questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client has a wound on the right heel and has eaten poorly for a month. Yesterday at 0800 the note read: redness 1 cm around the wound, mild swelling, no drainage, pain 2 of 10. Today at 0800 the redness extends 3 cm around the wound, the swelling has increased, the dressing holds thick yellow drainage (pus), and the client rates pain 6 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C. A new nurse says, "Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, so I will chart this as inflammation." Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Agree, document the findings as expected inflammation, and compare the heel again at 2000
options.rationale: The rule is quoted correctly, but it no longer fits. There is more than redness and swelling here: the drainage is new, and the redness, swelling, and pain are all worse.

options.text: Report the wider redness, new thick yellow drainage, and higher pain now as findings that suggest infection
options.rationale: Redness has spread from 1 cm to 3 cm, pain has risen from 2 to 6 of 10, and thick yellow drainage is new. Pus is a sign of local infection, and worsening findings are reported.

options.text: Clean away the drainage, apply a fresh dressing, and report if drainage appears again by 2000
options.rationale: Wound care is appropriate, but waiting for the drainage to return delays the report of findings that are already worse.

options.text: Report the findings once the oral temperature rises above the 36.8 °C measured this morning
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for a fever. The local findings have already changed.

questions.takeaway: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Spreading redness, rising pain, and new pus are more than that: they are worsening findings that suggest infection and are reported.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The new nurse's rule is true and it is the trap. Ask what the stem adds beyond redness and swelling, and whether the findings match yesterday.

steps.detail: Redness 1 cm to 3 cm. Pain 2 to 6 of 10. Drainage: none to thick yellow.

steps.action: Test the rule against the stem
steps.detail: "Alone" no longer applies. Drainage is new.
For more drainage, or for a fever.
It states the findings and what they suggest.

elimination.verdict: Report the wider redness, new drainage, and higher pain as findings that suggest infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client twisted the right knee stepping off a curb 1 day ago. The skin over the knee is intact. The knee is warm, red, and swollen, and the client rates the pain 5 of 10. Oral temperature is 36.8 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C).

The findings at the right knee are best explained by [[1]].

The swelling at the knee develops because [[2]].

On reassessment, the nurse would treat [[3]] as a finding that requires follow up.

options.text: inflammation without infection, a protective response to the injury
options.rationale: Inflammation can occur after an injury without infection. A twisted knee with intact skin fits this.

options.text: infection, because warmth, redness, and swelling are all present
options.rationale: Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection. Inflammation can occur without infection.

options.text: inflammation caused by microorganisms that entered at the time of injury
options.rationale: Inflammation is the right idea, but the skin is intact and nothing in the stem shows invasion by microorganisms.

options.text: an adaptive immune response directed at a specific antigen
options.rationale: Inflammation is part of innate immunity. It is a rapid, broad response that needs no prior exposure.

options.text: fluid moves from the blood vessels into the tissue around the injury
options.rationale: In the vascular response, vessels dilate, blood flow increases, and fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue, causing swelling.

options.text: microorganisms multiply in the tissue around the injury
options.rationale: This describes infection. Swelling after an injury comes from fluid leaving the vessels.

options.text: blood vessels at the site narrow and hold fluid in the tissue
options.rationale: The vessels dilate in the vascular response. Narrowing does not explain swelling.

options.text: scar tissue forms and replaces the damaged tissue
options.rationale: Scar formation belongs to tissue repair, the last stage. It does not cause the early swelling.

options.text: redness that has spread beyond the edge marked yesterday
options.rationale: Findings are compared with baseline, and worsening is reported. Redness spreading beyond the marked edge is a change from baseline.

options.text: warmth and swelling that are still present 1 day later
options.rationale: Warmth and swelling are cardinal signs of inflammation. Still being present 1 day after the injury is expected, not worsening.

options.text: pain that is now 4 of 10
options.rationale: Pain was 5 of 10 at baseline. A lower rating is not a worsening finding.

options.text: an oral temperature of 37.0 °C, up from 36.8 °C yesterday
options.rationale: Both readings are inside the stated reference range of 36.1 to 37.2 °C. A change inside the range is not worsening.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation is a protective response that can follow an injury without infection. Swelling comes from fluid leaving dilated vessels, and only a change from baseline that shows worsening is followed up.
questions.strategy: Every blank has an option that sounds clinical but adds something the stem does not say. Check each against the stem: intact skin, a clear injury, and a temperature inside the stated range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A twisted knee with intact skin points to inflammation without infection.
Fluid moves from dilated vessels into the tissue.
Only the finding that has worsened from baseline needs follow up.
Warmth and swelling at day 1 are expected; a temperature change inside the reference range is not worsening.

elimination.verdict: Inflammation without infection; fluid moves from the vessels into the tissue; redness that has spread beyond the marked edge.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.scenario: A nurse educator reviews findings from five clients with a new nurse. None of the clients has a temperature outside the reference range of 36.1 to 37.2 °C.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is consistent with inflammation without infection or suggests infection.

rows.text: A warm, swollen bruise on the left thigh 2 days after a fall, skin intact
rows.rationale: Inflammation can follow an injury without infection, and the skin is intact.

rows.text: Red, itchy skin on both hands after cleaning with a new chemical product without gloves, skin intact
rows.rationale: Inflammation can follow exposure to an irritant. Redness alone does not establish infection.

rows.text: A cut on the right index finger that is red, swollen, and now drains thick yellow fluid
rows.rationale: Thick yellow drainage is pus. Pus at a site is a sign of local infection, not a finding of inflammation alone.

rows.text: A blister on the right heel from new shoes, filled with clear fluid, covering skin unbroken
rows.rationale: Blister formation is an example of inflammation without infection.

rows.text: Redness around a sacral wound that has spread from 1 cm to 5 cm since yesterday, with pain rising from 3 to 6 of 10
rows.rationale: Extended redness around a wound and rising pain are worsening findings that suggest infection, even with a temperature inside the reference range.

questions.takeaway: Inflammation can follow injury, an irritant, or infection. Redness and swelling alone do not establish infection, while pus or redness that spreads around a wound suggests it.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: A normal temperature is the trap: it is true for every client and settles nothing. Decide each row by what is present at the site and whether it has changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A fall, a chemical, and new shoes are triggers that cause inflammation without infection.

steps.action: Look for more than redness and swelling
steps.detail: Pus and spreading redness point toward infection.
The temperature is in range for all five clients, so it separates none of them.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1, 2, and 4 are inflammation without infection. Rows 3 and 5 suggest infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client admitted 2 days ago takes an immunosuppressant. The admission note records intact skin on the right forearm with no redness or swelling. Today the client reports a new painful, swollen area on the right forearm. Place the nurse's actions in the order they are performed.

options.text: Compare the findings with the right forearm findings recorded on admission
options.rationale: Comparing with baseline follows the physical assessment, because the nurse needs today's findings to compare.

options.text: Ask when the area appeared and whether the right forearm was injured
options.rationale: Assessment begins with symptom onset, recent injury, and illness history.

options.text: Document the change and report the new findings as a worsening from baseline
options.rationale: Changes over time are documented and worsening is reported once the comparison shows it.

options.text: Assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and use of the right hand and forearm
options.rationale: The physical findings are gathered after the history so the nurse knows what to look for.

questions.takeaway: Ask about onset and injury; assess warmth, color, swelling, pain, and function; compare with baseline; document and report worsening.
questions.strategy: The report is tempting to move up because the client takes an immunosuppressant. A report needs findings and a comparison, so gather them first.

steps.detail: Ask about onset and injury.
Warmth, color, swelling, pain, and function of the right forearm.
Compare with the admission note, then document and report.

elimination.verdict: B, D, A, C.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse is planning closer assessment for clients on a medical unit whose immune protection may be reduced. Which clients does the nurse identify? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 6 week old infant admitted with a feeding problem
options.rationale: Infants have immature immune systems.

options.text: An 86 year old admitted after a fall who lives alone
options.rationale: Older adults face immunosenescence, which affects their ability to fight infections.

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained left ankle that is warm, red, and swollen
options.rationale: These are cardinal signs of inflammation after an injury. Inflammation is a protective response, not a factor that reduces immune protection.

options.text: A 41 year old who takes a daily antirejection drug after a kidney transplant
options.rationale: An antirejection drug suppresses the immune system, and immunosuppressants can affect immune function.

options.text: A 29 year old who received a measles vaccination 1 month ago
options.rationale: Vaccination produces artificial active immunity. It builds protection rather than reducing it.

options.text: A 52 year old who has eaten less than half of each meal for 1 month
options.rationale: Malnutrition impairs immune cell function.

questions.takeaway: Age and developmental stage, nutritional status, disease and overall health, medications, and environmental exposures affect immunity. Signs of inflammation and a recent vaccination do not reduce protection.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe the immune system working: a swollen ankle and a recent vaccination. Ask whether each option lowers protection or shows it in action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An infant and an 86 year old both qualify.
An antirejection drug and poor intake both lower protection.
An antirejection drug suppresses the immune system.

steps.action: Reject the immune system at work
steps.detail: Inflammation and vaccination are protective responses.

elimination.verdict: A, B, D, F.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A nurse receives report on four clients. The oral temperature reference range is 36.1 to 37.2 °C. Which client does the nurse assess first?

options.text: A 34 year old with a sprained left ankle; redness is 8 cm across and pain is 6 of 10, both the same as yesterday
options.rationale: The redness is large, but it and the pain match yesterday. Unchanged cardinal signs after an injury fit inflammation without infection.

options.text: A 58 year old with a right shin wound; redness grew from 2 to 3 cm and pain from 3 to 5 of 10 since yesterday
options.rationale: Redness and pain have both worsened since yesterday. A temperature is not needed before acting on a change at the site.

options.text: A 78 year old with a right hand wound and dementia; oral temperature 37.4 °C and confusion, both unchanged since admission yesterday
options.rationale: The reading is above the reference range and the client is confused, which pulls hard. The deciding cue is that both findings are unchanged since admission.

options.text: A 45 year old with a rash on both forearms after using a cleaning product; the rash is smaller than yesterday
options.rationale: Inflammation can follow an irritant, and a rash that is smaller than at baseline is not a worsening finding.

questions.takeaway: Priority goes to the client who has changed from baseline. A finding outside a range that has not changed is less urgent than a worsening one, and the nurse does not wait for fever.
questions.strategy: Two options pull hard: the only temperature above the range belongs to an older, confused client, while the other client has a modest change. The deciding cue is "unchanged since admission yesterday" against "since yesterday": unchanged findings wait, worsening findings come first.

steps.detail: Ankle unchanged, temperature and confusion unchanged, rash smaller, shin wound worse.

steps.action: Do not let one number decide
steps.detail: A temperature above range that has not changed is not new.
Assess the client whose findings have worsened.

elimination.verdict: Assess the client whose shin wound redness and pain have worsened since yesterday.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews findings for five clients on a medical unit. The oral temperature reference range is 36.1 to 37.2 °C.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is best described as inflammation without infection, colonization, or infection.

rows.text: A nasal swab taken on admission grows MRSA. The nose shows no redness, swelling, or drainage, and oral temperature is 36.8 °C.
rows.rationale: Colonization means microorganisms are present in tissues without causing symptomatic disease. MRSA was found, but there are no signs at the site and the temperature is inside the range.

rows.text: Sneezing, clear nasal drainage, and swollen nasal tissue return each spring when pollen counts rise. Oral temperature is 36.7 °C.
rows.rationale: Inflammation can follow exposure to an irritant. Allergic rhinitis is an example of inflammation that occurs without infection.

rows.text: A sore throat with swollen, tender lymph nodes in the neck. Oral temperature is 38.6 °C.
rows.rationale: Pharyngitis and lymphadenopathy often accompany infection, and a temperature above the reference range adds a sign of systemic involvement.

rows.text: A urine culture from a long term urinary catheter grows bacteria. The urine is clear, the client reports no pain, and oral temperature is 36.9 °C.
rows.rationale: Bacteria are present, but nothing in the stem shows symptomatic disease. An organism on a culture does not by itself establish infection.

rows.text: A wound on the left lower leg has redness that spread from 2 to 6 cm since yesterday and pus on the dressing. The wound culture grows MRSA. Oral temperature is 37.0 °C.
rows.rationale: Spreading redness and pus are signs of local infection. A temperature inside the range does not rule infection out.

questions.takeaway: Finding an organism is not the same as infection. Colonization has an organism and no symptomatic disease; infection has an organism that multiplies and causes signs; inflammation can occur with no organism at all.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: MRSA appears twice and a normal temperature appears four times. Neither settles a row. Decide each row by whether the site shows signs of disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rows 1 and 4 have an organism and no signs: colonization.

steps.action: Find the trigger without an organism
steps.detail: Row 2 follows pollen exposure: inflammation without infection.
Row 3 has lymph node swelling and a temperature above range; row 5 has spreading redness and pus: infection.

elimination.verdict: Rows 1 and 4 are colonization. Row 2 is inflammation without infection. Rows 3 and 5 are infection.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: A client was admitted yesterday with acute pancreatitis. Current findings: oral temperature 38.4 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C), heart rate 112 beats/min (reference range 60 to 100 beats/min), respiratory rate 22 breaths/min (reference range 12 to 20 breaths/min), and white blood cell (WBC) count 13,500 per mm3 (reference range 5000 to 10,000 per mm3). No source of infection has been found. Blood cultures drawn on admission show no growth so far. The client is alert and oriented, as on admission, oxygen saturation is 97% (reference range 95 to 100%), and urine output is 60 mL/hr (reference range at least 30 mL/hr). A new nurse says, "This meets SIRS criteria, so the client has sepsis." Which response by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "SIRS criteria are met here, so sepsis is present and the antimicrobial is given within 1 hour."
options.rationale: SIRS describes a widespread inflammatory response and can occur with noninfectious causes such as pancreatitis. SIRS alone does not establish sepsis.

options.text: "This is widespread inflammation. Sepsis also needs infection with organ dysfunction, not shown here."
options.rationale: Sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction. Mentation matches admission, oxygen saturation and urine output are inside their ranges, and no infection source has been found.

options.text: "Sepsis can be ruled out, because no organism has been found in the client's blood cultures at this point."
options.rationale: An organism does not need to be found in the bloodstream for sepsis to be present. The diagnosis is clinical, based on signs of organ dysfunction.

options.text: "These findings point to early sepsis, because the respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min is now above 20 breaths/min."
options.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min is concerning and is trended. Alone it does not show organ dysfunction when mentation, oxygen saturation, and urine output are inside their ranges.

questions.takeaway: SIRS is inflammation spread through the body, and pancreatitis can cause it without infection. Sepsis needs infection plus organ dysfunction, so look for new confusion, poor oxygenation, or falling urine output.
questions.strategy: Option D is the pull: a respiratory rate above 20 breaths/min is a sepsis cue on the slides. The deciding cue is that every marker of organ function in the stem, mentation, oxygen saturation, and urine output, is at baseline or inside its range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pancreatitis is a noninfectious cause of SIRS.
"Ruled out" ignores that sepsis is a clinical diagnosis.
Mentation at baseline, oxygen saturation 97%, urine output 60 mL/hr: none shown.
It is concerning and is trended, but one number does not establish sepsis.

elimination.verdict: SIRS alone is not sepsis; sepsis needs infection with organ dysfunction, and none is shown.

questions.objective: Differentiate inflammation from infection

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client has a draining wound on the right foot that was cultured 3 days ago. Today the white blood cell (WBC) count is 16,800 per mm3 (reference range 5000 to 10,000 per mm3) and band neutrophils are 12% (reference range up to 5%). Oral temperature is 37.0 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C).

The rise in band neutrophils shows [[1]].

This matters because [[2]].

The nurse uses these results by [[3]].

options.text: the marrow releasing immature neutrophils because it cannot keep up with a continuing infection
options.rationale: A left shift means more immature band neutrophils are circulating because the marrow cannot keep up with a continuing infection.

options.text: adaptive immunity forming memory cells that target the organism in the wound
options.rationale: Memory cells come from B and T lymphocytes. Band cells are immature neutrophils, part of innate defense.

options.text: an allergic response, with cells that defend against parasites rising
options.rationale: Eosinophils rise in allergic responses and defend against parasites. The result given is bands, not eosinophils.

options.text: the expected pattern of the tissue repair stage as the wound heals
options.rationale: Tissue repair is the last stage. A rise in immature neutrophils signals continuing infection, not repair.

options.text: immature neutrophils cannot perform phagocytosis, so fewer cells can engulf the organism
options.rationale: Only mature neutrophils can phagocytose. More immature cells in circulation means less ability to engulf and destroy the organism, and a left shift is seen in sepsis.

options.text: band neutrophils produce the antibodies that bind to the organism in the wound
options.rationale: Antibodies come from plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes. Neutrophils do not make antibodies.

options.text: band neutrophils release histamine that dilates the vessels around the wound
options.rationale: Basophils and mast cells release histamine. This describes the vascular response, not a left shift.

options.text: immature neutrophils live longer than mature ones and keep the response going
options.rationale: Nothing in the sources supports this. The concern with bands is that they cannot phagocytose.

options.text: interpreting them together with the wound findings and the client's baseline
options.rationale: Results are interpreted together with the client's assessment and compared with baseline.

options.text: waiting until the temperature rises above 37.2 °C before acting on them
options.rationale: Infection can be present without fever, and the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: using the WBC count alone to decide whether an infection is present
options.rationale: The WBC count adds information about the immune response, but no single result replaces the assessment.

options.text: repeating the count in 24 hours before reporting, because one result can be a laboratory error
options.rationale: A rise in bands signals that the marrow cannot keep up. Waiting a day to repeat the count delays the response, and the result is read with the wound findings now.

questions.takeaway: A left shift means the marrow is sending out immature neutrophils that cannot phagocytose, a sign the body is losing ground to a continuing infection. Read the results now with the wound and the baseline, not alone, not by temperature, and not after a day of waiting.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Each wrong option in blanks 1 and 2 describes a real immune cell or stage, just not the band neutrophil. Match the result to the cell it names: bands are immature neutrophils.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Bands are immature neutrophils.
Mature neutrophils engulf bacteria; immature ones cannot.
Antibodies belong to plasma cells, histamine to basophils and mast cells, memory to lymphocytes.

steps.action: Place the result in the assessment
steps.detail: Interpret with the wound findings and baseline, without waiting for fever.

elimination.verdict: The marrow is releasing immature neutrophils for a continuing infection; immature cells cannot phagocytose; interpret with the wound findings and baseline.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.scenario: A client was admitted 2 days ago with an infected wound on the left lower leg. At 0800 the client was alert and oriented, respiratory rate was 18 breaths/min, and heart rate was 88 beats/min. At 1400 the client is restless and asks where they are. Respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min (reference range 12 to 20 breaths/min), heart rate is 118 beats/min (reference range 60 to 100 beats/min), and urine output is 40 mL over the past 2 hours (reference range at least 30 mL/hr). Oral temperature is 37.1 °C (reference range 36.1 to 37.2 °C).
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process now
options.rationale: When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately to the provider or the rapid response process.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mental status, and vital signs
options.rationale: Reassessing breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs is an immediate action when sepsis is suspected.

options.text: Recheck the temperature in 1 hour and escalate if it is above 37.2 °C
options.rationale: The nurse does not wait for fever. New confusion, a rising respiratory rate, and falling urine output are already present.

options.text: Mark the edge of the wound redness and compare it at the next dressing change
options.rationale: Comparing the site with baseline is right in general, but the changes now are in breathing, mentation, and urine output, and they cannot wait.

options.text: Possible sepsis arising from the infected leg wound
options.rationale: An infected wound plus new confusion, a rising respiratory rate, and urine output below range are early cues of sepsis.

options.text: Local wound infection without effects beyond the leg
options.rationale: The wound is infected, but new confusion and falling urine output show effects beyond the leg.

options.text: Inflammation at the wound without any infection
options.rationale: The stem states the wound is infected, and the new findings are systemic.

options.text: Anxiety about the hospital stay causing restlessness
options.rationale: Anxiety does not explain urine output below its reference range. New confusion is compared with the 0800 baseline and treated as a sepsis cue.

options.text: Mental status compared with the 0800 baseline
options.rationale: Sudden changes in mental status may indicate sepsis and are compared with baseline behavior.

options.text: Urine output each hour
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of adequate perfusion and is tracked during suspected sepsis.

options.text: Oral temperature as the main sign of change
options.rationale: Temperature is one finding. The nurse judges the whole trend and does not rely on fever alone.

options.text: Pain rating at the wound on the left lower leg
options.rationale: Pain at the site matters, but the key monitoring areas in suspected sepsis are alertness, blood pressure, perfusion, breathing, and urine output.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is an immune response to infection that has become uncontrolled and disrupts organ function. New confusion, faster breathing, and falling urine output are the early cues, and a temperature inside the range does not delay escalation.
questions.strategy: The temperature inside the range is the trap. Name the condition from the changes since 0800: mentation, respiratory rate, heart rate, and urine output. Actions and parameters then follow from suspected sepsis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Alert to restless and disoriented; respiratory rate 18 to 28; heart rate 88 to 118; urine output 20 mL/hr.
An infected wound with organ dysfunction cues points to possible sepsis.
Escalate now and reassess breathing, circulation, and mentation.
Mentation against baseline and hourly urine output.

elimination.verdict: Possible sepsis; escalate now and reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs; monitor mental status against baseline and hourly urine output.

questions.objective: Connect immune responses with nursing assessment

questions.stem: A client receiving treatment that suppresses the immune system is on neutropenic precautions. This morning the client develops frequent liquid stools, and the provider suspects C. difficile. The stool test result will not be available until tomorrow. Which action does the nurse take when preparing to give care?

options.text: Continue neutropenic precautions today and add contact precautions when the result is confirmed
options.rationale: Contact precautions are right, but the timing is wrong. They are started for suspected as well as confirmed C. difficile.

options.text: Replace neutropenic precautions with contact precautions and wear a gown and gloves for all contact
options.rationale: Gown and gloves are right, but precautions are added, not swapped. The client still needs protective precautions.

options.text: Continue neutropenic precautions and start contact precautions now, with gown and gloves for all contact
options.rationale: Contact precautions are initiated for suspected or confirmed C. difficile, with gown and gloves during all client contact. The client's protective precautions continue.

options.text: Continue neutropenic precautions and add a mask for all care until the result is available
options.rationale: A mask is for droplet spread. C. difficile calls for contact precautions with gown and gloves.

questions.takeaway: Start contact precautions for suspected or confirmed C. difficile, with gown and gloves for all contact. Precautions are added to what the client already needs, never swapped.
questions.strategy: Two decisions are packed into each option: what happens to the precautions the client already has, and when and how the new ones start.

steps.detail: Neutropenic precautions in place. C. difficile suspected, result tomorrow.
Suspected or confirmed, so start now.
Contact: gown and gloves, not a mask.

steps.action: Check what happens to the first set
steps.detail: It continues.

elimination.verdict: Continue neutropenic precautions and start contact precautions now.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.stem: A nurse finishes care for a client on neutropenic precautions and contact precautions for suspected C. difficile. Facility policy states that soap and water is used after care of clients with suspected or confirmed C. difficile. The nurse's gloves are intact and the hands are not visibly soiled. How does the nurse complete hand hygiene?

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, then wash with soap and water before going on to the next client
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after gloves are removed, and for C. difficile soap and water is used when facility policy indicates it.

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, then use alcohol based sanitizer because the hands are not visibly soiled
options.rationale: Sanitizer is preferred in most routine situations when hands are not visibly soiled. Here the facility policy for C. difficile directs soap and water.

options.text: Wash the gloved hands with soap and water, then remove the gown and gloves and go to the next client
options.rationale: Soap and water is right, but the order is wrong. Hands are cleaned after the gloves come off.

options.text: Remove the gown and gloves, use alcohol based sanitizer now, and wash with soap and water before eating
options.rationale: Washing before eating is correct in general, but it does not replace the hand hygiene the policy requires now.

questions.takeaway: Clean hands after removing gloves. Sanitizer is preferred for routine care when hands are not visibly soiled, but for C. difficile use soap and water when facility policy indicates it.
questions.strategy: "Not visibly soiled" and "gloves intact" both point toward sanitizer. The stated policy for C. difficile overrides the routine choice, and the order of glove removal settles the rest.

steps.detail: Not visibly soiled: sanitizer is usually preferred.

steps.action: Find the exception in the stem
steps.detail: Facility policy: soap and water after C. difficile care.
Gloves come off first, then hands are cleaned.

elimination.verdict: Remove gown and gloves, then wash with soap and water.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.stem: A client receiving treatment that suppresses the immune system is on neutropenic precautions and contact precautions for suspected C. difficile. The client is tearful and asks to see a family member. The family member arrives and says, "My allergies are acting up, so I have had a runny nose and a little cough since yesterday. I brought a mask and I will stay only a few minutes." Which action is best?

options.text: Have the family member put on a mask, gown, and gloves and clean the hands, then allow a visit of a few minutes
options.rationale: Protective equipment does not make an ill visitor safe for this client. The visitor reports new symptoms, and the nurse cannot confirm the cause. A short visit still exposes the client.

options.text: Explain that visitors are screened for illness, ask the family member to wait until well, and offer a phone call now
options.rationale: Neutropenic precautions include screening visitors and staff for illness. The nurse explains this in plain language and still responds to the client's wish for contact.

options.text: Ask the client to decide, because the client understands the risk and has asked for the visit
options.rationale: Involving the client is usually right, but screening visitors for illness is part of the precautions that protect this client.

options.text: Allow the family member to stand in the doorway in a mask, away from the bed, for a few minutes
options.rationale: Distance and a mask do not make an ill visitor safe for a client on neutropenic precautions.

questions.takeaway: Neutropenic precautions protect the client: protective precautions as indicated, meticulous hand hygiene, and screening visitors and staff for illness.
questions.strategy: Protective equipment sounds like enough, and the client's distress pulls toward allowing the visit. The visitor's own explanation, allergies, makes the symptoms sound harmless. The deciding cue is that screening is for symptoms, and this visitor has a runny nose and a cough that began yesterday.

steps.detail: The client, by the neutropenic precautions.
Runny nose and cough since yesterday, whatever the visitor thinks the cause is.
Equipment, distance, and client choice do not remove the exposure.

steps.action: Meet the client's need another way
steps.detail: Explain plainly and offer contact that carries no exposure.

elimination.verdict: Explain the screening, ask the family member to wait until well, and offer a phone call.

questions.objective: Select standard and transmission-based precautions

questions.nursesNote: 1400, day 2 of admission for pneumonia: Restless and pulling at bed linen, calm and alert at 1000. Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 at 1000. Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, same as at 1000. Oral temperature 37.1 °C. Urine output 25 mL per hour, was 60 mL per hour at 1000. Productive cough, unchanged since admission.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that suggest possible sepsis.

segments.text: Restless and pulling at bed linen, calm and alert at 1000
segments.rationale: A new change in mental status in a client with an infection is an early cue of sepsis.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, was 18 at 1000
segments.rationale: A respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute is concerning, and this is a rise from baseline.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 95% on room air, same as at 1000
segments.rationale: The value matches baseline.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C
segments.rationale: This reading is not a cue by itself, and it does not rule sepsis out. The nurse does not rely on fever alone.

segments.text: Urine output 25 mL per hour, was 60 mL per hour at 1000
segments.rationale: Decreased urine output signals deterioration.

segments.text: Productive cough, unchanged since admission
segments.rationale: The cough is an expected finding of pneumonia and has not changed.

questions.takeaway: Early cues of sepsis in a client with an infection: new confusion or restlessness, a respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute, temperature changes, and decreased urine output. Fever is not required.
questions.strategy: Look for change from the 1000 baseline in mentation, breathing, and urine output. An unchanged finding of the pneumonia itself is not a new cue.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Pneumonia.
Mentation, respiratory rate, urine output.
Oxygen saturation and cough.

steps.action: Do not lean on the temperature
steps.detail: 37.1 °C neither adds a cue nor removes the others.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has become restless over the past 4 hours. The respiratory rate has risen from 18 to 26 breaths per minute and urine output has fallen from 60 to 25 mL per hour. The nurse has just assessed the client, found these changes, and suspects sepsis. Place the nurse's next actions in order.

options.text: Give the prescribed treatment promptly and reassess the client's response
options.rationale: Treatment is given once it is prescribed, and the nurse then checks whether it worked.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process
options.rationale: Escalation comes first when sepsis is suspected, so that help and orders are on the way.

options.text: Obtain the ordered specimens and check that the intravenous access works
options.rationale: Ordered specimens are collected before the antimicrobial is started when that does not delay it, and working access lets treatment begin without delay.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs while help is on the way
options.rationale: The first assessment is already done. This is the reassessment while help is on the way, so that current findings are ready to report.

questions.takeaway: When sepsis is suspected: escalate immediately, reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs, obtain ordered specimens and check intravenous access, then give prescribed treatment promptly and reassess. Specimens come before the antimicrobial only when collecting them does not delay it.
questions.strategy: The stem says the assessment has been done and the cues are in hand, so the first move is to escalate. Reassessment follows while help is on the way, and treatment comes after the specimens.

steps.detail: The cues are already in hand, so call first.
Breathing, circulation, mentation, vital signs.
Ordered specimens are obtained and the line is checked.
Give what is prescribed, then check the response.

elimination.verdict: Notify, reassess, obtain specimens and check access, treat and reassess.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.scenario: A client is on day 2 of admission for pneumonia. At 1000 the client was calm and alert with a heart rate of 88 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and urine output of 60 mL per hour. At 1400 the client is restless, the heart rate is 112 beats per minute, the respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute, urine output is 25 mL per hour, and the oral temperature is 37.1 °C. No new orders have been written.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Notify the provider or activate the rapid response process now
options.rationale: When sepsis is suspected, the nurse escalates immediately.

options.text: Reassess breathing, circulation, mentation, and vital signs
options.rationale: The nurse reassesses these while help is on the way.

options.text: Recheck the oral temperature in 1 hour and escalate if a fever develops
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable, but the nurse does not wait for fever. Several cues are already present.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and reassess urine output at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Supporting hydration is appropriate in general, but it is not a response to a falling urine output with other cues of sepsis.

options.text: Possible sepsis
options.rationale: A client with an infection has a new mental status change, a faster heart rate, a respiratory rate above 20, and decreased urine output.

options.text: Expected course of pneumonia
options.rationale: New restlessness and a fall in urine output are changes from baseline, not expected findings.

options.text: Anxiety about the hospital stay
options.rationale: Restlessness with faster breathing and less urine in a client with an infection is not treated as anxiety.

options.text: Inflammation without infection
options.rationale: The client has a known infection, and the findings show body systems working worse than at baseline.

options.text: Mental status compared with the 1000 baseline
options.rationale: Mental status moving toward baseline is a marker of improvement.

options.text: Urine output each hour
options.rationale: Urine output is a key marker of adequate perfusion.

options.text: Amount and color of sputum
options.rationale: Sputum describes the pneumonia. It does not show whether perfusion is improving.

options.text: Oral temperature every 4 hours as the main measure
options.rationale: Temperature is trended, but the nurse does not rely on it alone. Mentation and urine output show perfusion.

questions.takeaway: Infection plus new changes in mentation, breathing, and urine output is possible sepsis. Escalate and reassess, then follow mental status, blood pressure and perfusion, urine output, and breathing.
questions.strategy: Name the condition from the changes since 1000, not from the temperature. The actions are the first two steps for suspected sepsis, and the parameters are the markers of perfusion.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Known infection plus four changes from baseline.
Escalate now and reassess. Options that wait are out.
Choose markers of perfusion and mentation, not descriptions of the pneumonia.

elimination.verdict: Possible sepsis; escalate and reassess; monitor mental status and hourly urine output.

questions.objective: Recognize early cues of sepsis and septic shock

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia was treated for suspected sepsis 2 hours ago with the prescribed antimicrobial and intravenous fluids. By the time treatment began the client was restless and confused, blood pressure was 96/58 mm Hg, the respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, both feet were cool and mottled, and urine output was 20 mL per hour. Now blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg and the respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute. The client is still confused, both feet are still cool and mottled, and urine output is still 20 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Continue the current plan and reassess in 15 minutes, because blood pressure and breathing are both better
options.rationale: Two numbers are better, but the nurse judges the whole trend. Mentation, skin, and urine output have not changed.

options.text: Report the better blood pressure and breathing now, and hold the other findings for the next update
options.rationale: A report that leaves out the unchanged findings hides the reason for concern.

options.text: Warm both feet with blankets and recheck the skin before deciding whether the other findings need a call
options.rationale: Warming addresses one finding and delays action on persistent poor perfusion.

options.text: Notify the provider of the current findings now and ask for the plan to be reviewed
options.rationale: Mentation, skin findings, and urine output are considered together with blood pressure and breathing. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend rather than one number: mentation, blood pressure, skin findings, breathing, and urine output together. Persistent signs of poor perfusion require further escalation.
questions.strategy: A better blood pressure is the most reassuring number there is, and breathing is better too. The deciding cue is that the three findings that show perfusion at the tissues have not moved.

steps.detail: Better: blood pressure, respiratory rate. Unchanged: mentation, skin, urine output.
Mentation, skin color and temperature, urine output.
A recheck in 15 minutes fits a client improving across the board. Two hours after treatment, this client is not.
Persistent poor perfusion: escalate further.

elimination.verdict: Notify the provider of the current findings now.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client with pneumonia was treated for suspected sepsis 6 hours ago. By the time treatment began the client was restless and confused, the respiratory rate was 26 breaths per minute, both feet were cool and mottled, and urine output was 20 mL per hour. Which set of findings now shows that the client is improving?

options.text: Oral temperature is 37.0 °C, the client is still confused, and urine output is 20 mL per hour
options.rationale: One number in range does not show improvement when mentation and urine output have not changed.

options.text: Client is alert and oriented, respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, and urine output is 55 mL per hour
options.rationale: Mental status has moved toward baseline, breathing has slowed from 26 to 20, and urine output has risen from 20 to 55 mL per hour. Every finding given points the same way.

options.text: Client is alert and oriented, respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute, and both feet are cool and mottled
options.rationale: Mentation and breathing are better, but cool, mottled skin is a sign of poor perfusion. The whole trend has to improve.

options.text: Respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, and the client now responds only when shaken
options.rationale: A slower rate with a drop in responsiveness is not improvement. Mental status has moved away from baseline.

questions.takeaway: Judge the whole trend: mental status toward baseline, blood pressure and perfusion improving, urine output improving, breathing and oxygenation stabilizing.
questions.strategy: Two options start with the same good findings. Read to the end of each: one finishes with a sign of poor perfusion and one with a better urine output.

steps.detail: Confusion, respiratory rate 26, cool mottled feet, urine 20 mL per hour.

steps.action: Check each option to the end
steps.detail: Only one has every finding moving the right way.
A normal temperature, a slower rate, or two good findings with mottled skin is not improvement.

elimination.verdict: Alert and oriented, respiratory rate 20, urine output 55 mL per hour.

questions.objective: Describe immediate nursing actions when sepsis is suspected

questions.stem: A client had surgery on the right lower leg 4 days ago and has had an indwelling urinary catheter since the operation. The provider's orders include strict intake and output. The unit has no nurse driven protocol for catheter removal. The client now walks to the bathroom with one person assisting and is eating and drinking. During morning care the nurse reviews the client's devices. Which action does the nurse take about the catheter?

options.text: Leave the catheter in place, because the order for strict intake and output requires accurate measurement
options.rationale: The order is for measurement, not for a catheter. A client who walks to the bathroom can have output measured another way.

options.text: Leave the catheter in place, and increase catheter care to twice each shift to lower the risk
options.rationale: Catheter care helps prevent exposure, but it does not answer whether the device is still needed.

options.text: Raise with the provider whether the catheter is still needed, and offer to measure output another way
options.rationale: The nurse reassesses whether urinary catheters are still needed. This client walks and drinks, and the reason given for the catheter can be met without it.

options.text: Remove the catheter this morning, because the nurse decides when a device is no longer needed
options.rationale: Questioning the device is right. Removing it without an order or a protocol goes beyond what the situation supports.

questions.takeaway: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers. Reassess whether urinary catheters and vascular access devices are still needed, and raise it when the reason for the device can be met another way.
questions.strategy: The order for strict intake and output makes keeping the catheter look required. Separate what was ordered, which is measurement, from the device, and then stay within the nurse's role.

steps.detail: Day 4, walks to the bathroom, drinking.

steps.action: Separate the order from the device
steps.detail: Output can be measured without a catheter.

steps.action: Compare the two options that question the device
steps.detail: One raises it with the provider. One removes it without an order.

elimination.verdict: Raise whether the catheter is still needed and offer another way to measure output.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A client had surgery on the right lower leg 5 days ago, and the surgical wound is now draining. The provider orders a wound culture and a first dose of an antimicrobial, both to be done this morning. The antimicrobial is at the bedside and due now, and the culture swab has to be brought from the supply room. The client is alert, with a respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute and a blood pressure of 124/76 mm Hg, which matches the readings from the past 2 days. In which order does the nurse carry out the orders?

options.text: Obtain the wound culture, then give the first dose of the antimicrobial
options.rationale: The culture identifies the organism and guides treatment. It is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

options.text: Give the first dose of the antimicrobial, then obtain the wound culture
options.rationale: Both actions are right, but the order is reversed. The specimen is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

options.text: Obtain the wound culture and hold the antimicrobial until the result is reported
options.rationale: The culture comes first, but treatment is not held for the result. Treatment of the suspected cause is given as ordered.

options.text: Give the first dose of the antimicrobial and obtain the culture only if the wound does not improve
options.rationale: The culture was ordered to guide treatment from the start. It is not kept in reserve.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides treatment. Collect the specimen before the antimicrobial is started when that causes no meaningful delay, and do not hold treatment for the result. In probable sepsis the antimicrobial is not delayed for cultures.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: The drug is ready and the swab is not, which pulls toward giving the dose first. The client's vital signs match baseline, so there is time to collect the specimen first.

steps.detail: Options that hold or skip an order are out.

steps.action: Compare the two that do both
steps.detail: Culture first, or antimicrobial first.
The specimen is collected before the antimicrobial is started.

elimination.verdict: Culture first, then the antimicrobial.

questions.scenario: A client has cellulitis of the right leg with a draining wound, and the wound culture is positive for MRSA. A second client, in the next room, has a central venous catheter in the right chest and receives treatment that suppresses the immune system. The nurse cares for both clients today.
questions.stem: For each nursing action, indicate the link in the chain of infection that the action interrupts.

rows.text: Giving the first client the prescribed antimicrobial for the MRSA cellulitis
rows.rationale: Treating the infection acts on the organism where it lives, in the first client's wound.

rows.text: Keeping the draining wound on the first client's right leg covered with an intact dressing
rows.rationale: Organisms leave the reservoir through the wound. Containing the drainage closes that exit.

rows.text: Performing hand hygiene after removing gloves in the first client's room
rows.rationale: Hands carry organisms from one client to the next. Clean hands break that route, even though the second client is the one who will be touched next.

rows.text: Using a blood pressure cuff kept only for the first client's room
rows.rationale: Shared equipment carries organisms between clients. Dedicated equipment removes the vehicle.

rows.text: Asking the provider whether the second client's central venous catheter is still needed
rows.rationale: A central line bypasses the skin and gives organisms a direct path into the bloodstream. Removing an unneeded device closes that entry.

rows.text: Offering the second client the recommended vaccines before discharge
rows.rationale: Vaccination lowers the second client's risk for the infections the vaccines cover, which makes the host less susceptible.

questions.takeaway: The chain runs agent and reservoir, portal of exit, method of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Every infection control action works by breaking one link, and naming the link tells you why the action matters.
questions.strategy: Follow the organism's path from the first client's wound to the second client. Ask where the organism is at the moment each action happens: still in the wound, leaving it, traveling, entering, or meeting a host.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It lives in the first client's wound: treating it acts on the agent and reservoir.
The draining wound; a covered dressing contains it.
Hands and the cuff both carry organisms between rooms.

steps.action: Find the entry and the host
steps.detail: The central line is the entry. Vaccination changes the host.

elimination.verdict: Agent and reservoir; portal of exit; transmission; transmission; portal of entry; susceptible host.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.nursesNote: 0800, day 2 of admission for cellulitis of the right lower leg; wound culture positive for MRSA; receiving the prescribed antimicrobial. Redness now extends 3 cm beyond the skin marking drawn at admission. Right calf warm and swollen, unchanged since admission. Small amount of yellow drainage on the dressing, same as yesterday. Heart rate 108 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100), was 84 at admission. Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20), same as admission. Oral temperature 37.1 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Blood pressure 116/74 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), same as admission. Asks the same question three times in 10 minutes; alert and oriented at admission.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings the nurse reports promptly.

segments.text: Redness now extends 3 cm beyond the skin marking drawn at admission
segments.rationale: The infection is spreading past the border marked at admission while the client receives the antimicrobial. A worsening site is reported.

segments.text: Right calf warm and swollen, unchanged since admission
segments.rationale: Warmth and swelling are expected with cellulitis, and they match admission.

segments.text: Small amount of yellow drainage on the dressing, same as yesterday
segments.rationale: The drainage has not changed from yesterday.

segments.text: Heart rate 108 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100), was 84 at admission
segments.rationale: The heart rate is above the reference range and has risen from 84 at admission, a change in circulation in a client with an infection.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20), same as admission
segments.rationale: The rate is within the reference range and matches admission.

segments.text: Oral temperature 37.1 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C)
segments.rationale: The reading is within the reference range. It is not a cue by itself, and it does not cancel the other changes, because the nurse does not rely on fever alone.

segments.text: Blood pressure 116/74 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), same as admission
segments.rationale: The blood pressure is within the reference range and matches admission.

segments.text: Asks the same question three times in 10 minutes; alert and oriented at admission
segments.rationale: This is a new change in mental status compared with the admission baseline, a change that matters in a client with an infection.

questions.takeaway: Compare each finding with the client's baseline. A spreading site, a rising heart rate, and new confusion are reported even when the temperature is within range.
questions.strategy: Sort every finding into changed or unchanged since admission. Expected findings of cellulitis that have not changed are not new cues, and a normal temperature does not cancel the findings that have changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Redness past the marking, heart rate 84 to 108, new repeated questions.
Warmth and swelling, drainage, respiratory rate, blood pressure.

steps.action: Do not lean on the temperature
steps.detail: 37.1 °C neither adds a cue nor removes the others.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: A client with cellulitis of the right leg is being discharged with a dressing over a draining wound. The wound culture was positive for MRSA, and the client has a prescription for an oral antibiotic. The client lives with a partner and a 6 year old child. Which statements by the client indicate that the teaching has been effective? Select all that apply.

options.text: "This germ spreads by touch, from the wound or from things the drainage has touched."
options.rationale: MRSA is spread by contact: touching the person, the wound, or contaminated items.

options.text: "Because this germ spreads by touch, my family only needs to clean their hands if they touch the wound itself."
options.rationale: Contact is the right route, but it is too narrow. Items the drainage has touched also spread MRSA, so hands are cleaned after touching those too.

options.text: "I will clean my hands after I touch the dressing, even if I wore gloves."
options.rationale: Hands are cleaned after gloves are removed, because gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

options.text: "When my hands look dirty after a dressing change, hand sanitizer is enough."
options.rationale: Cleaning the hands is right, but the method is wrong. Visibly soiled hands are washed with soap and water.

options.text: "I will take every dose of the antibiotic, even once my leg looks better."
options.rationale: The whole course is completed. Stopping early when the leg looks better leaves organisms behind.

options.text: "I will save any leftover pills in case my child catches a cold this winter."
options.rationale: Antibiotics do not treat viral infections such as a cold, unnecessary use adds to resistance, and leftover pills mean the course was not finished.

questions.takeaway: Teach MRSA as a contact organism: clean hands after touching the wound or dressing and after removing gloves, soap and water when hands are visibly soiled, finish the whole antibiotic course, and never use antibiotics for a viral illness.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: Two wrong statements have the right idea with one fact off: contact limited to the wound in one, the hand hygiene method in the other. Check the reach of contact, the method, and the antibiotic use in each statement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contact includes items the drainage touched, not only the wound.
Visibly dirty hands need soap and water.
Finish the course; a cold is viral.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client who is 84 years old has chronic kidney disease, receives immunosuppressive treatment, and has a central venous catheter in the right chest and an abdominal surgical incision from 3 months ago that is closed with no redness or drainage. The nurse identifies [[1]] as the factors that increase this client's risk for infection by lowering the body's defenses.

The nurse identifies [[2]] as the factor that bypasses the body's natural barriers.

If this client develops an infection, the nurse expects that [[3]].

options.text: the client's age, the immunosuppressive treatment, and the central venous catheter
options.rationale: Age and the treatment lower immune status, but the catheter does not lower defenses. It bypasses the barriers, and chronic kidney disease is left out.

options.text: the chronic kidney disease, the immunosuppressive treatment, and the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Chronic illness and the treatment lower immune status, but the incision is closed with no redness or drainage, so the skin barrier is intact, and age is left out.

options.text: the client's age, the chronic kidney disease, and the immunosuppressive treatment
options.rationale: Age extremes, chronic illness, and immunosuppressive treatment all lower immune status.

options.text: the abdominal incision
options.rationale: Broken skin gives direct access to pathogens, but this incision is closed with no redness or drainage.

options.text: the central venous catheter
options.rationale: Invasive devices bypass natural barriers and give organisms a direct path into the bloodstream.

options.text: the immunosuppressive treatment
options.rationale: The treatment raises risk by lowering immune status, not by bypassing a barrier.

options.text: a fever will be the first sign, so the temperature is checked every 2 hours
options.rationale: Checking temperature is part of assessment, but fever is not relied on as the first or only sign.

options.text: a fever may not appear, so changes in behavior and function from baseline matter
options.rationale: Immune status shapes the response. The nurse does not rely on fever alone and watches for changes from baseline.

options.text: the white blood cell count will rise before other findings appear
options.rationale: A count is interpreted together with the assessment, and a client with low immune status may not mount the usual rise, so no single lab result is waited on.

questions.takeaway: Immune status drives infection risk: age extremes, chronic illness, and immunosuppressive treatment. Invasive devices and broken skin open a direct path in. In a client with low immune status, do not wait for a fever.
questions.strategy: Sort the client's factors into two groups: those that weaken the defenses and those that open a path past them. A factor belongs in only one group. Then ask what weak defenses do to the signs you expect to see.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Age 84, chronic kidney disease, and the treatment all lower immune status.
The central line bypasses them. The incision is closed with no redness or drainage, so the skin is intact.
Fever may be absent, so compare with baseline. No single lab result replaces the assessment.

elimination.verdict: Age, chronic kidney disease, and the treatment; the central venous catheter; fever may not appear.

questions.objective: Identify patient factors that increase infection risk

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four clients at 1200. Reference ranges: oral temperature 36.1 to 37.2 °C, heart rate 60 to 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 12 to 20 breaths per minute, urine output at least 30 mL per hour. Which client's findings fit sepsis rather than infection alone or an inflammatory response alone?

options.text: Acute pancreatitis, no source of infection found: oral temperature 38.4 °C, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, alert, urine output 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: Temperature, heart rate, and respiratory rate are all outside the reference ranges, which is an inflammatory response. No infection has been found, and sepsis requires infection plus organ dysfunction.

options.text: Urinary tract infection and dementia: oral temperature 38.1 °C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, confused as on admission, urine output 45 mL per hour
options.rationale: Infection with a fever is present, but the confusion matches the admission baseline, and the other findings are within range. No new organ dysfunction is shown.

options.text: Cellulitis of the left leg, redness spread 2 cm since 0800: oral temperature 37.1 °C, heart rate 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, alert, urine output 50 mL per hour
options.rationale: The local infection is worsening, which raises the risk for sepsis, but every finding outside the leg is within range. No organ dysfunction is shown.

options.text: Urinary tract infection: oral temperature 37.0 °C, heart rate 92 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, confused since 1000 after being alert, urine output 40 mL per hour
options.rationale: Infection plus a new change in mental status is evidence of organ dysfunction. Sepsis can be present without a fever or abnormal vital signs.

questions.takeaway: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction, such as new confusion. An inflammatory response alone does not establish sepsis, and sepsis can occur without abnormal temperature, heart rate, or respiratory rate.
questions.strategy: The client with the most abnormal numbers looks sickest, and the client with dementia also has an infection and confusion. The deciding cue is the word new: only one client's confusion began today after being alert.

steps.detail: Pancreatitis with no infection found shows inflammation, not sepsis.
Mental status, oxygenation, urine output.
One is confused as on admission. One became confused since 1000.
Infection with a fever and fast heart rate meets SIRS but is not sepsis without new organ dysfunction.
Spreading redness alone with every other finding in range is not organ dysfunction.

elimination.verdict: The client with a urinary tract infection and new confusion since 1000.
