questions.scenario: A nurse on a medical unit cares for several clients with infections during one shift.
questions.stem: For each situation, indicate the route by which the organism reaches the next person.

rows.text: A client with a draining wound on the left leg sits in a wheelchair, and a second client uses the same wheelchair before it is cleaned
rows.rationale: The organism travels on a contaminated item. Shared equipment touched by wound drainage is a contact route.

rows.text: A client with a respiratory infection coughs while a visitor sits at the bedside, and droplets reach the visitor's nose and mouth
rows.rationale: Respiratory droplets reach the mucous membranes of a person nearby.

rows.text: A client with a respiratory infection coughs into both hands, then presses the call light, which the nurse touches next without gloves
rows.rationale: The organism started in a cough, but it reached the nurse on a contaminated item. The route is the way it reaches the next person, and here that is touch.

rows.text: A client with a cough leaves the room for a test. A staff member who enters 30 minutes later, touches nothing, and never meets the client develops the same infection
rows.rationale: The client was gone and nothing was touched. Only particles that stay suspended in the air can explain the spread.

rows.text: A client sneezes during an assessment, and droplets land in the nurse's eyes
rows.rationale: The eyes are a mucous membrane. Droplets that reach a nearby person's mucous membranes spread by the droplet route.

rows.text: A client with a respiratory infection is placed in a shared room. The roommate, whose bed is across the room and who never comes near the client or touches anything the client used, becomes ill with the same infection
rows.rationale: Droplets travel short distances, and there was no contact. Spread across a room points to particles suspended in the air.

questions.takeaway: Contact spreads by touching a person or a contaminated item, droplet by respiratory droplets reaching nearby mucous membranes, and airborne by particles that stay suspended in the air. Name the route by how the organism reaches the next person, not by where it came from.
questions.strategy: A cough does not make the route droplet. Ask how the organism reached the next person: by touch, by droplets at close range, or by particles still in the air.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The shared wheelchair and the call light are both contaminated items.

steps.action: Look for close range and mucous membranes
steps.detail: The visitor's nose and mouth, the nurse's eyes.
A person who enters 30 minutes later and touches nothing, or one across the room who never comes near, points to airborne spread.
The cough into the hands spreads by contact.

elimination.verdict: Contact; droplet; contact; airborne; droplet; airborne.

questions.objective: Explain how infection spreads to a susceptible person

questions.stem: A client, 78 years old, is admitted from the emergency department with a cough and suspected pneumonia. The client lives at home with a family member. Oral temperature 37.0 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C), heart rate 96 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20 breaths per minute), oxygen saturation 93% on room air (reference 95 to 100%). Which actions belong in the nurse's admission infection assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask when the cough started and how it has changed since then
options.rationale: Symptoms and their onset are part of the history in an infection assessment.

options.text: Ask whether anyone the client lives or works with has been ill recently
options.rationale: Exposures are part of the history and can point to the source.

options.text: Ask whether any devices are in place, such as a urinary catheter used at home
options.rationale: Devices are part of the history. They bypass natural barriers and can be a source of infection.

options.text: Ask the family member how the client's alertness and activity compare with usual
options.rationale: Findings are compared with the client's baseline. Changes in behavior and function matter, and the family member knows what is usual.

options.text: Obtain a sputum specimen for culture before finishing the history, so the organism is identified quickly
options.rationale: The nurse obtains ordered specimens. No culture has been ordered, and the history is part of the assessment, not a step to cut short.

options.text: Record the oxygen saturation of 93% as expected for a client who is 78 years old
options.rationale: 93% is below the reference range of 95 to 100%. Decreased oxygen saturation is a concerning cue, and age does not make it expected.

questions.takeaway: The infection assessment gathers symptoms, onset, exposures, recent treatment, and devices; assesses overall appearance, the likely site, and respiratory status; and compares every finding with baseline. Do not rely on fever alone.
questions.strategy: The two wrong options each sound like good practice: one rushes to identify the organism, and one explains a low value by age. Ask whether the specimen was ordered and whether the value is inside its reference range.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Onset, exposures, and devices all belong.
Comparing with usual alertness and activity belongs.
No culture was ordered, and the history is not cut short.
93% is below 95 to 100%, whatever the age.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D.

questions.objective: Assess for infection and recognize clinical deterioration

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client has a draining wound on the left foot. The provider orders a wound culture and susceptibility, a complete blood count with differential, and an intravenous antimicrobial. The nurse explains that the culture and susceptibility test [[1]].

The nurse explains that the complete blood count with differential [[2]].

On day 2, the susceptibility report shows that the organism is resistant to the antimicrobial the client is receiving, and the next dose is due in 1 hour. The nurse [[3]].

options.text: adds information about how the immune system is responding
options.rationale: This describes the complete blood count with differential, not the culture.

options.text: identifies the organism and helps guide which antimicrobial is used
options.rationale: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides treatment.

options.text: shows where in the body the infection has spread
options.rationale: Other tests and imaging may help locate an infection. The culture identifies the organism.

options.text: adds information about the immune response, read together with the assessment
options.rationale: The complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response, and results are interpreted together with the client's assessment.

options.text: confirms the infection, so the wound assessment can be done less often
options.rationale: A lab result is read together with the assessment. It does not replace it.

options.text: shows whether the infection has spread beyond the wound
options.rationale: Other tests and imaging may help locate an infection or assess its effects. The blood count adds information about the immune response.

options.text: gives the next dose on time, because a missed dose lowers the drug level, and then reports the result
options.rationale: On time dosing matters, but this drug may not treat the organism. The provider needs the report before the dose so the order can change.

options.text: holds the next dose and waits for the provider to see the report on rounds
options.rationale: Questioning the dose is right, but holding it without reporting leaves the client with no treatment and no new plan.

options.text: reports the result to the provider before the next dose is due
options.rationale: The nurse supports appropriate antimicrobial use by following culture results, and the provider needs the result to change the treatment.

questions.takeaway: Culture and susceptibility identifies the organism and guides the antimicrobial choice. The complete blood count with differential adds information about the immune response. Read every result together with the assessment, and act on a susceptibility report that does not match the drug being given.
questions.strategy: Match each test to the question it answers: which organism and which drug, or how the body is responding. For the last blank, look for the choice that both protects the client from an ineffective drug and gets a new plan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Which organism, which drug.
How the immune system is responding, read with the assessment.
Do not give the dose first or hold it silently. Report before the dose is due.

elimination.verdict: Identifies the organism and guides treatment; adds information about the immune response; reports the result before the next dose.

questions.objective: Explain the nurse's role in testing, treatment, and teaching

questions.stem: A client admitted with a urinary tract infection was alert at 0700 and is confused at 0900. Oral temperature 38.6 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C), heart rate 112 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute (reference 12 to 20 breaths per minute), blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg). At 0915 the provider examines the client, documents probable sepsis without shock, and orders blood cultures and an intravenous antimicrobial. Facility policy states that laboratory staff draw blood cultures, and they report that they can reach the unit at 1115. The antimicrobial arrives at 0930, and the intravenous access works. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give the antimicrobial at 1115 right after the laboratory staff draw the blood cultures
options.rationale: Specimens are obtained before the antimicrobial when that causes no delay, and 1115 is within 3 hours. The 3 hour window is for possible sepsis without shock. Probable sepsis calls for the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour, and waiting for cultures until 1115 delays it 2 hours.

options.text: Hold the antimicrobial, recheck vital signs every 30 minutes, and give it if the blood pressure falls
options.rationale: Rechecking vital signs is right, but waiting for a falling blood pressure waits for shock. The provider has documented probable sepsis, which calls for the antimicrobial now.

options.text: Draw blood for culture from the existing intravenous line, then give the antimicrobial now
options.rationale: Getting the specimen first is the right idea, but facility policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff, and the existing line is not the way the specimen is obtained.

options.text: Give the antimicrobial now, and have the blood cultures drawn when the laboratory staff arrive
options.rationale: For probable sepsis the antimicrobial is given immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Cultures come first only when drawing them delays the antimicrobial by no more than 45 minutes; here the delay would be 2 hours.

questions.takeaway: Probable or definite sepsis, or septic shock: give the antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: investigate rapidly and begin treatment within 3 hours if concern persists. Obtain cultures first only when that does not delay the antimicrobial.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in Lecture PPT. The detail tested is covered in Reading (Iggy).
questions.strategy: "Without shock" and the culture first habit both point toward waiting until 1115, which is still inside 3 hours. The deciding cue is the provider's word probable: the 3 hour window belongs only to possible sepsis without shock.

steps.detail: The provider documented probable sepsis, not possible sepsis.
Probable sepsis: antimicrobial immediately, ideally within 1 hour.
Cultures first is right only when it causes no delay. A 2 hour wait is a delay.
A falling blood pressure is not required to act.
Policy assigns blood cultures to laboratory staff.

elimination.verdict: Give the antimicrobial now and draw cultures when the laboratory staff arrive.

skills.title: Cardiac Assessment
skills.subtitle: Pulse and apical pulse, cardiac monitoring, recording and reading a 12 lead ECG, heart sounds, and a heart failure home visit

questions.stem: A nurse needs an apical pulse on an adult client with large breasts before giving digoxin. The nurse palpates the left chest and cannot feel an impulse. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Ask the client to lift the left breast, listen at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line, and count for 1 full minute
options.rationale: The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line. A client with large breasts is asked to lift the breast. The impulse cannot be felt in every client, and the count is still made by listening for 1 full minute.

options.text: Use the radial pulse instead, because the apical impulse cannot be felt, and count for 1 full minute
options.rationale: A full minute is right, but the site is wrong. An impulse that cannot be felt is not a reason to change sites, and the apical pulse is heard, not only felt.

options.text: Place the diaphragm at the 2nd intercostal space to the right of the sternum and count for 1 full minute
options.rationale: A full minute with the diaphragm is right, but this is the aortic area. The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line.

options.text: Ask the client to lift the left breast, listen at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line, count 30 seconds, and double it
options.rationale: The site and the breast are handled correctly, but the apical pulse before digoxin is counted for 1 full minute.

questions.takeaway: The apical pulse is at the 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line. Listen with the diaphragm for 1 full minute. Ask a client with large breasts to lift the breast. Not feeling the impulse is not a reason to switch sites.
questions.strategy: Each option gets something right, and two options match on site and breast. Check the site first, then the length of the count.

steps.detail: 5th intercostal space, left midclavicular line.
1 full minute, by listening.
The client lifts the breast.
An impulse that cannot be felt is common and expected in some clients.

elimination.verdict: Have the client lift the breast, listen at the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line, and count 1 full minute.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: A nurse is locating the apical pulse on an adult client by landmarks. Place the steps in order.

options.text: Move just to the left of the sternum into the 2nd intercostal space
options.rationale: The 2nd intercostal space lies just beside the angle of Louis, so it is the first space the nurse can name with certainty.

options.text: Find the sternal notch between the clavicles
options.rationale: The sternal notch is the starting landmark.

options.text: Place the diaphragm and count for 1 full minute
options.rationale: Listening comes after the site is found, and the count is a full minute.

options.text: Find the angle of Louis, the ridge on the sternum
options.rationale: The angle of Louis is the next landmark below the notch.

options.text: Count down to the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line
options.rationale: From the 2nd space, the nurse counts down the spaces along the midclavicular line to the 5th.

questions.takeaway: To find the apical pulse: sternal notch, angle of Louis, 2nd intercostal space just to the left, then down the midclavicular line to the 5th space, then listen for 1 full minute.
questions.strategy: Start with the landmark that cannot be mistaken, the notch, and let each step name the next one. The space cannot be counted until the 2nd space has been found.

steps.detail: The sternal notch.
The angle of Louis comes next, below the notch.
2nd intercostal space, just left of the angle of Louis.
Midclavicular line to the 5th space, then listen.

elimination.verdict: Notch, angle of Louis, 2nd space, down the midclavicular line to the 5th space, listen for 1 full minute.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: Digoxin is due at 0900 for an adult client. The nurse listens at the 5th intercostal space on the left midclavicular line for 1 full minute and counts an apical pulse of 56 beats per minute, regular. Blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. The client is alert and says, "My pulse is always in the fifties. My doctor knows about it." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Give the digoxin, because the client has no symptoms and the provider is aware of the usual rate
options.rationale: The client's report and the lack of symptoms matter, but the rate is below the range wanted before digoxin. The nurse does not decide alone that a low rate is acceptable.

options.text: Hold the digoxin and report the apical rate of 56 beats per minute now, with the client's statement about the usual rate
options.rationale: Before digoxin the heart rate should be within 60 to 100 beats per minute. At 56 beats per minute the dose is held, and the report gives the provider both the rate and the client's statement so that a decision can be made.

options.text: Hold the digoxin, document the apical rate of 56 beats per minute, and recheck the apical pulse before the next scheduled dose
options.rationale: Holding is right, but a held dose and the reason are reported at the time. Whether a rate in the fifties is acceptable for this client is the provider's decision, and without a report the client simply misses the medication.

options.text: Count the apical pulse for 1 more full minute, and give the digoxin if the second count is 60 beats per minute or more
options.rationale: The first count was already a full apical minute with a regular rhythm. A second count only looks for a number that permits the dose.

questions.takeaway: Count the apical pulse for 1 full minute before digoxin. The adult range wanted is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Below 60, hold the dose and report.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Two options hold the dose. The deciding cue is who may accept a rate below 60 beats per minute: the provider, today, not the nurse and not the next shift.

steps.detail: Apical 56 beats per minute for a full minute.
60 to 100 beats per minute before digoxin.
It is reported, not acted on alone.
One reports now. One leaves the decision until the next dose.

elimination.verdict: Hold the digoxin and report the rate with the client's statement.

questions.objective: Outline the location of different pulse points and the process for undertaking an accurate pulse assessment

questions.stem: A client is to be placed on continuous cardiac monitoring. The client's chest is damp with sweat and has thick hair where the electrodes will go. The client is awake and able to answer questions. Which action does the nurse take to prepare the skin?

options.text: Dry the skin and press the electrodes firmly over the hair, securing each one with tape
options.rationale: Drying is right, but hair still prevents good contact, and tape does not fix that.

options.text: Explain the monitoring, shave the electrode sites with the client's consent, and apply the electrodes to the damp skin
options.rationale: Consent and hair removal are right, but the skin must be dry.

options.text: Dry the skin, and with the client's consent shave the hair where the electrodes will be placed
options.rationale: Skin should be clean and dry with good contact. With the client's consent, chest hair may be shaved to allow contact.

options.text: Dry the skin and shave the electrode sites, then explain to the client why the hair was removed
options.rationale: Both problems are solved, but consent comes before shaving. This client is awake and able to answer.

questions.takeaway: For cardiac monitoring the skin must be clean and dry with good electrode contact. Chest hair may be shaved, with the client's consent.
questions.strategy: Check three things in each option: dry skin, hair removed, and consent given first.

steps.detail: Moisture and hair.

steps.action: Drop options that leave one unsolved
steps.detail: Tape over hair, or damp skin.

steps.action: Compare the two that solve both
steps.detail: Consent before shaving, or explanation after.

elimination.verdict: Dry the skin and, with consent, remove hair at the electrode sites.

questions.nursesNote: 1030, review of a 12 lead ECG recorded as a routine baseline: Calibration box is 2 large squares high and speed is 25 mm per second. One P wave comes before each QRS complex. PR interval is 7 small squares on every beat. QRS width is 2 small squares. R waves are evenly spaced, 4 large squares apart. ST segment is raised above the baseline in leads II, III and aVF.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that are outside the expected range and must be reported.

segments.text: Calibration box is 2 large squares high and speed is 25 mm per second
segments.rationale: This is the standard calibration: 1 millivolt equals 2 large squares, and the speed is 25 mm per second.

segments.text: One P wave comes before each QRS complex
segments.rationale: One P wave per QRS is the expected finding.

segments.text: PR interval is 7 small squares on every beat
segments.rationale: The PR interval should be 3 to 5 small squares. Consistently longer could indicate first degree heart block.

segments.text: QRS width is 2 small squares
segments.rationale: The QRS should be 3 small squares or less, so 2 small squares is within range.

segments.text: R waves are evenly spaced, 4 large squares apart
segments.rationale: The rhythm is regular, so 300 divided by 4 gives 75 beats per minute, within the adult range of 60 to 100 beats per minute.

segments.text: ST segment is raised above the baseline in leads II, III and aVF
segments.rationale: ST elevation could indicate myocardial infarction. Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall of the heart.

questions.takeaway: Read an ECG in order: clean trace, calibration, rhythm, one P per QRS, measurements (PR 3 to 5 small squares, QRS 3 or less, rate by the 300 rule), then scan for ST and T wave changes.
questions.strategy: Take each line of the note as one of the six steps and test it against its normal. Two lines fail: one measurement and one finding from the scan.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 2 large squares and 25 mm per second: correct.
PR 7 is long. QRS 2 is in range. 300 divided by 4 is 75 beats per minute.
ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF needs review now.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: A nurse records a 12 lead ECG on a client who has reported palpitations. The client was talking and shifting on the examination table during the recording, and the printout has a thick, wavy baseline in most leads. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Send the printout for interpretation with a note that the client was moving during the recording
options.rationale: A note is honest, but interference should be sorted at the point of recording. A poor trace can hide or mimic changes.

options.text: Replace all of the electrodes with new ones and record the ECG again straight away
options.rationale: Recording again is right, but the cause is movement and talking. New electrodes do not remove it, and the second trace will look the same.

options.text: Mark the rate from the R waves that can be seen and report the palpitations with that rate
options.rationale: Reporting palpitations is right, but a rate taken from a poor trace may be wrong, and the trace can be fixed now.

options.text: Ask the client to lie still with the hands relaxed at the sides and not to talk, then record the ECG again
options.rationale: The first step in reading an ECG is a clean trace. Interference is fixed at the time of recording, so the cause is removed and the ECG is recorded again.

questions.takeaway: Step 1 of reading a 12 lead ECG is a clean trace. Fix interference at the point of recording and record again if in doubt.
questions.strategy: Two options record again. Only one removes the cause stated in the stem, movement and talking.

steps.detail: Talking and moving during the recording.

steps.action: Ask whether it can be fixed now
steps.detail: Yes: the client lies still and the ECG is repeated.

steps.action: Drop the options that miss the cause
steps.detail: A note, an estimated rate, or new electrodes.

elimination.verdict: Have the client lie still and quiet, and record again.

questions.objective: Describe why a 12 lead ECG might be used in practice and how to undertake the procedure of recording one for a patient

questions.stem: A client reports chest pain that began 20 minutes ago and rates it 6 of 10. A 12 lead ECG recorded 5 minutes ago shows a clean trace, correct calibration, and no ST elevation in any lead. The client still rates the pain 6 of 10. A colleague says, "There is no ST elevation. Let the client rest." Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Record a second 12 lead ECG now so that two traces can be compared, then report the chest pain with both ECGs
options.rationale: Repeat ECGs are real practice, but the first trace is 5 minutes old, clean and correctly calibrated. A second recording delays the report of pain that has lasted 20 minutes.

options.text: Stay with the client, measure pulse and blood pressure, and report the chest pain after reassessing it in 15 minutes
options.rationale: Staying and measuring are right, but the pain has already been reassessed and is unchanged at 6 of 10. Waiting 15 minutes delays the report.

options.text: Report the ongoing chest pain and the ECG now, and ask a clinician competent in ECG interpretation to review it
options.rationale: A myocardial infarction can be present without ST elevation. The pain is unchanged, so the nurse reports now and has the ECG reviewed by a competent clinician.

options.text: Check the lead placement and record the 12 lead ECG again, because the first one may have been inaccurate
options.rationale: The trace was clean and correctly calibrated. Nothing in the situation suggests a recording error, and repeating it delays the report.

questions.takeaway: ST elevation could indicate myocardial infarction, but an infarction can be present without it. Ongoing chest pain is reported, and a competent clinician reviews the ECG.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Three options do something useful before reporting. The deciding cues are that the pain is unchanged at 6 of 10 after 20 minutes and that the ECG is already clean and 5 minutes old, so nothing needs to come before the report.

steps.action: Separate the ECG from the client
steps.detail: ECG: no ST elevation. Client: pain still 6 of 10.
An infarction can be present without ST elevation.
A repeat ECG and vital signs are useful, but not before the report.
Clean trace and correct calibration.

elimination.verdict: Report the ongoing chest pain and the ECG now for review.

questions.scenario: A home health nurse visits a 76 year old client with heart failure. The client's furosemide was increased from 40 mg to 80 mg once a day last week because of weight gain and swollen ankles. The client's spouse weighs the client every morning and keeps the record. The client also takes simvastatin 80 mg at night.
questions.stem: For each finding at today's visit, indicate whether it is an expected finding or requires follow-up.

rows.text: Weight is 2 kg lower than before the dose was increased
rows.rationale: The diuretic was increased to remove extra fluid. A lower weight shows it is working.

rows.text: The client reports feeling light headed when standing up from the bed
rows.rationale: A doubled diuretic can remove too much fluid. Light headedness on standing is a new symptom that needs assessment and reporting.

rows.text: Respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 97% and no increased shortness of breath
rows.rationale: These findings show no sign that fluid is affecting the breathing.

rows.text: The client says the simvastatin has been skipped for the last 3 nights
rows.rationale: Medication adherence is part of the assessment. A missed medication is explored and addressed with the client.

rows.text: Right radial pulse is 62 beats per minute and regular, the right hand is warm, and capillary refill is 2 seconds
rows.rationale: The rate is within 60 to 100 beats per minute, the rhythm is regular, and the limb is well perfused.

rows.text: The spouse is tearful and says, "I am not sleeping. I lie awake listening to the breathing."
rows.rationale: A holistic assessment includes the wellbeing of the family. A caregiver who is not sleeping needs attention and support.

questions.takeaway: After a diuretic increase, a lower weight with a respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, pulse and capillary refill in range is expected. New light headedness on standing, missed medication, and a caregiver who is not sleeping each need follow-up.
questions.coverage: Topic covered in the skill course. The detail tested is standard NCLEX teaching, not from the course.
questions.strategy: Sort the findings into what the dose was meant to achieve and what is new or going wrong. Follow-up is not only for abnormal vital signs: adherence and the caregiver count too.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Name the goal of the change
steps.detail: Less fluid: lower weight, less swelling.
All in range.
A new symptom, a missed medication, and a tearful caregiver.

elimination.verdict: The lower weight, the breathing findings, and the right radial pulse findings are expected. Light headedness, skipped simvastatin, and the spouse's distress require follow-up.

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: A home health nurse is beginning a visit with a 76 year old client with heart failure whose diuretic dose was increased last week. The nurse wants to learn how the client has been managing since the change. Which opening by the nurse is best?

options.text: "You have been taking the new dose every morning since it went up, haven't you?"
options.rationale: This is a leading question. It invites the client to agree and makes a missed dose harder to admit.

options.text: "Tell me how things have been for you at home since your water pill was increased."
options.rationale: An open question lets the client describe what matters most, including problems the nurse did not think to ask about.

options.text: "How is your breathing today compared with last week?"
options.rationale: This is open, but it covers one symptom on one day, not how the client has been managing since the change.

options.text: "What side effects have you noticed since your water pill was increased?"
options.rationale: This is open in form, but it limits the answer to side effects and assumes there are some.

questions.takeaway: Open questions let the client tell the nurse how things are going. A leading question or a question limited to one topic narrows what the client will say.
questions.strategy: Three options are questions the client can answer at length. Match each to the stated goal: how the client has been managing since the change.

steps.detail: "Haven't you?" invites agreement.
One asks only about breathing today.
One assumes side effects.
"Tell me how things have been."

elimination.verdict: "Tell me how things have been for you at home since your water pill was increased."

questions.objective: Interpret the findings from a patient assessment to identify the priorities for planning care

questions.stem: A nurse is listening to the heart of a 76 year old client with heart failure. Respiratory rate is 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 97%, and the client reports no increased shortness of breath. At the 2nd intercostal space to the left of the sternum, the nurse hears the second heart sound as two close sounds when the client breathes in and as a single sound when the client breathes out. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Report the finding now as a new abnormal heart sound in a client with heart failure
options.rationale: Reporting is right for a new abnormal sound, but a second heart sound that splits only on inspiration is a normal finding.

options.text: Move the stethoscope to the 5th intercostal space at the left midclavicular line, where the second heart sound is loudest
options.rationale: The second heart sound is loudest at the aortic and pulmonary areas, where the nurse already is. The mitral area is where the first heart sound is best heard.

options.text: Document a murmur at the pulmonary area and ask for the client to be reviewed at the next routine visit
options.rationale: A murmur is an extra sound. Here the second heart sound itself divides, and only on breathing in, which is a normal finding and not a murmur.

options.text: Document the second heart sound as split on inspiration and single on expiration, and continue the assessment
options.rationale: On inspiration more blood returns to the right side of the heart, so the pulmonary valve closes slightly after the aortic valve. This physiologic splitting of the second heart sound is expected.

questions.takeaway: S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, loudest at the 2nd intercostal spaces. A split on inspiration that disappears on expiration is physiologic and expected.
questions.strategy: A client with heart failure and an unusual sound pulls toward reporting. The deciding detail is the timing: two sounds only on breathing in.

steps.detail: S2, heard at the pulmonary area.
Split on inspiration, single on expiration.
Physiologic splitting is expected.
S2 is loudest at the base, not the apex.

elimination.verdict: Document the split on inspiration and continue the assessment.

questions.objective: Identify how to undertake cardiac auscultation and what these sounds represent in relation to the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: A client with an irregular left radial pulse of 104 beats per minute (expected adult range 60 to 100 beats per minute) is to start continuous cardiac monitoring with a 5 lead system. The client has heart failure and is awake. Which actions by the nurse are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Select lead II for the monitor display, because its waveform is easily interpreted
options.rationale: Lead II is usually selected for monitoring because it is easily interpreted.

options.text: Place the right arm electrode just below the right clavicle, near the right shoulder
options.rationale: The right arm electrode sits under the right clavicle near the shoulder, on the chest and inside the rib cage frame.

options.text: Place the leg electrode on the left upper thigh, below the level of the umbilicus
options.rationale: The leg electrode is placed on the chest, at the lower edge of the left rib cage below the pectoral muscles, not on the limb.

options.text: Place the chest electrode at the 4th intercostal space, left sternal margin
options.rationale: The space is right but the side is wrong. On a 5 lead system this electrode sits at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin.

options.text: Set the alarm limits according to this client's clinical condition
options.rationale: Alarm limits are set based on the client's clinical condition, so they warn of change that matters for this client.

options.text: Leave the lower heart rate alarm at the unit default, because the client's rate is above the expected range
options.rationale: A rate above the range today does not make the lower limit irrelevant, and a default limit ignores the client's condition. Every alarm limit is set based on this client's clinical condition.

questions.takeaway: For continuous monitoring: lead II on display, electrodes on the chest within the rib cage frame, the 5th electrode at the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin, and alarm limits set to the client's condition.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement on its own. For electrode positions, check two things: is it on the chest inside the rib cage frame, and is it on the correct side.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lead II, easily interpreted: correct.
Right arm under the right clavicle is correct. The leg electrode belongs on the lower left rib cage. The chest electrode belongs at the right sternal margin.
Set to the client's condition, not left at default.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.objective: Consider when cardiac monitoring may be used for a patient and how the clinician might apply this

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a newly recorded 12 lead ECG for a client admitted with palpitations. Place the steps in the order the nurse reviews the ECG.

options.text: Measure the PR interval and the QRS width, and calculate the heart rate
options.rationale: Measurements come after the rhythm and the P to QRS relationship are known, because the method for the rate depends on whether the rhythm is regular.

options.text: Confirm that the trace is clean and free of interference
options.rationale: A clean trace comes first. Interference can hide or mimic changes, and it is fixed at the time of recording.

options.text: Scan every lead for ST elevation, ST depression, T wave inversion and tall R waves
options.rationale: Scanning the leads for changes is the last step.

options.text: Check that the calibration box is 2 large squares high and the speed is 25 mm per second
options.rationale: Calibration is checked before any measurement, because every square counted depends on it.

options.text: Check that there is one P wave for every QRS complex
options.rationale: This follows the rhythm check. More P waves than QRS complexes could indicate second or third degree heart block.

options.text: Look at the lead II rhythm strip to decide whether the rhythm is sinus
options.rationale: The rhythm is judged from the rhythm strip, normally lead II, once the trace and calibration are confirmed.

questions.takeaway: Read a 12 lead ECG in six steps: clean trace, calibration, sinus rhythm, one P wave per QRS, measurements, then scan the leads.
questions.strategy: Ask what each step depends on. Nothing can be read on a poor trace, nothing can be measured without correct calibration, and the rate method depends on whether the rhythm is regular.

steps.detail: Clean first, then calibration.
Lead II strip, then one P wave per QRS.
PR, QRS and rate.
ST and T wave changes, tall R waves.

questions.stem: A client on continuous cardiac monitoring reports palpitations. The nurse prints a lead II rhythm strip recorded at 25 mm per second. The spaces between R waves vary from 2 to 4 large squares with no pattern. The first two R waves are 3 large squares apart. The nurse counts 12 R waves within 30 large squares. The expected adult heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Which heart rate does the nurse record?

options.text: 120 beats per minute, by counting the 12 R waves in 30 large squares and multiplying by 10
options.rationale: With an irregular rhythm the rate is found by counting the R waves in 30 large squares, which is 6 seconds, and multiplying by 10. This gives 120 beats per minute, above the expected range.

options.text: 100 beats per minute, by dividing 300 by the 3 large squares between the first two R waves
options.rationale: The 300 rule is a correct method, but only for a regular rhythm. Here the spacing varies from 2 to 4 large squares, so one pair of R waves does not represent the rate, and the result falsely sits inside the expected range.

options.text: 75 beats per minute, by dividing 300 by the 4 large squares of the widest R to R space
options.rationale: The widest space gives the slowest beats only. With an irregular rhythm, no single R to R space gives the rate.

options.text: 110 beats per minute, by counting the 11 spaces between R waves in 30 large squares and multiplying by 10
options.rationale: The 6 second method and the multiplier are right, but the method counts R waves, not the spaces between them. 12 R waves have only 11 spaces, so this undercounts by 1 beat in every 6 seconds.

questions.takeaway: Use 300 divided by the large squares between R waves only when the rhythm is regular. When it is irregular, count the R waves in 30 large squares (6 seconds) and multiply by 10.
questions.strategy: Two methods are both correct ways to calculate a rate. The deciding cue is in the stem: the R to R spacing varies with no pattern, so the rhythm is irregular and only the 6 second count applies.

steps.detail: R to R spacing varies from 2 to 4 large squares: irregular.
Any 300 rule answer uses one space that does not represent the rate.
30 large squares is 6 seconds, so multiply by 10.
12 R waves times 10 is 120 beats per minute, above 60 to 100.

elimination.verdict: 120 beats per minute, from 12 R waves in 30 large squares multiplied by 10.

questions.scenario: A client with chest pain rated 7 of 10 has a 12 lead ECG recorded. While the nurse reports the chest pain, a clinician competent in ECG interpretation reviews the trace with the nurse. Each finding below is reviewed by lead group.
questions.stem: For each ECG finding, indicate the coronary artery that supplies the area of the heart those leads look at.

rows.text: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF
rows.rationale: Leads II, III and aVF are the inferior leads, which look at the area supplied by the right coronary artery.

rows.text: ST elevation in leads V3 and V4
rows.rationale: V3 and V4 are the anterior leads, which look at the area supplied by the left anterior descending artery.

rows.text: ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6
rows.rationale: Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, which look at the area supplied by the left circumflex artery.

rows.text: ST elevation in leads V1 and V2
rows.rationale: V1 and V2 are the septal leads. Like the anterior leads, they look at the area supplied by the left anterior descending artery.

rows.text: T wave inversion in leads V5 and V6
rows.rationale: V5 and V6 are lateral leads, even though they are chest leads. The lateral group is supplied by the left circumflex artery.

questions.takeaway: Inferior leads II, III and aVF: right coronary artery. Lateral leads I, aVL, V5 and V6: left circumflex. Septal V1 and V2 and anterior V3 and V4: left anterior descending.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding by its leads, not by whether it is ST elevation, ST depression or T wave inversion. The type of change does not move the territory.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: II, III, aVF inferior. I, aVL, V5, V6 lateral. V1, V2 septal. V3, V4 anterior.
Inferior: right coronary. Lateral: circumflex. Septal and anterior: left anterior descending.
V5 and V6 are chest leads but belong to the lateral group.

elimination.verdict: II, III, aVF: right coronary. V3, V4 and V1, V2: left anterior descending. I, aVL, V5, V6 and V5, V6: left circumflex.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse auscultates the heart of an adult client lying back with the diaphragm of the stethoscope. The nurse identifies the "lub" sound. This sound is produced by closure of [[1]].

It marks [[2]].

The nurse expects it to be loudest at [[3]].

options.text: the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.rationale: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves produces the second heart sound, which is short and sharp.

options.text: the mitral and tricuspid valves
options.rationale: The first heart sound is the atrioventricular valves, the mitral and tricuspid, closing.

options.text: the mitral and aortic valves
options.rationale: Both are left sided valves, but they close at different times. The aortic valve closes with the pulmonary valve in the second heart sound.

options.text: the tricuspid and pulmonary valves
options.rationale: Both are right sided valves, but the pulmonary valve closes in the second heart sound.

options.text: the start of diastole
options.rationale: The second heart sound marks the start of diastole.

options.text: atrial contraction at the end of diastole
options.rationale: Atrial contraction happens at the end of diastole, before the first heart sound. It does not produce the first heart sound.

options.text: the start of systole
options.rationale: When the ventricles begin to contract, the atrioventricular valves close, so the first heart sound marks the start of systole.

options.text: the end of systole
options.rationale: The end of systole is when the aortic and pulmonary valves close, producing the second heart sound.

options.text: the 2nd intercostal space at the right upper sternal border
options.rationale: This is the aortic area, where the second heart sound is loudest.

options.text: the 2nd intercostal space at the left upper sternal border
options.rationale: This is the pulmonary area, where the second heart sound is loudest.

options.text: the 5th intercostal space near the left midclavicular line
options.rationale: This is the mitral area. The first heart sound is best heard at the mitral and tricuspid areas.

options.text: the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal margin
options.rationale: This is not an auscultation area. The tricuspid area is beside the left lower sternal border.

questions.takeaway: S1 is the mitral and tricuspid valves closing at the start of systole, long and loud, best heard at the mitral and tricuspid areas. S2 is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing at the start of diastole, loudest at the 2nd intercostal spaces.
questions.strategy: Fix the valves first. Once S1 is tied to the atrioventricular valves, the timing (they close as the ventricles contract) and the site (the lower areas named after those valves) follow.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The lub sound is the first heart sound: mitral and tricuspid closing.
These valves close as the ventricles contract: start of systole.
Loudest at the mitral area, 5th intercostal space near the left midclavicular line.

elimination.verdict: Mitral and tricuspid valves; the start of systole; the 5th intercostal space near the left midclavicular line.

questions.stem: A 12 lead ECG is ordered for an adult client whose left radial pulse is 112 beats per minute and irregular (expected adult range 60 to 100 beats per minute). The client is awake, able to answer questions, and has not had an ECG before. Which actions does the nurse take while preparing the client and placing the electrodes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Confirm the client's name and date of birth before starting
options.rationale: Identity is confirmed with the name and date of birth before the recording, so the trace belongs to the right client.

options.text: Ask whether the client has any chest pain at this moment
options.rationale: The course lists asking about chest pain as part of preparing for the recording, and chest pain is one of the listed reasons for a 12 lead ECG.

options.text: Ask the client to sit upright on the edge of the bed with the hands resting in the lap
options.rationale: Relaxed hands are right, but the position is wrong. The client lies back on the bed with the hands relaxed and flat at the sides, which reduces movement interference.

options.text: Place the 4 limb electrodes on the chest inside the rib cage frame, as for continuous monitoring
options.rationale: Inside the rib cage frame is the placement for continuous monitoring. For a 12 lead ECG the 4 limb electrodes go on the wrists and ankles.

options.text: Palpate the chest to locate the landmarks for the chest electrodes
options.rationale: The chest is palpated to find the landmarks for the chest electrodes, so each one is placed accurately.

options.text: Apply the electrodes first, then explain the procedure and gain consent before pressing record
options.rationale: Explanation and consent are right, but they come before the client is touched. This client is awake and able to answer.

questions.takeaway: Before a 12 lead ECG: confirm name and date of birth, explain and gain consent, ask about chest pain, have the client lie back with the hands relaxed flat at the sides, palpate the chest for landmarks, and place the limb electrodes on the wrists and ankles.
questions.strategy: Check each option for the one detail that is off: the position, the limb electrode site, or the point at which consent is gained.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Name and date of birth first; consent before touching the client.
Chest pain now is asked about.
Lying back, hands relaxed flat at the sides, not sitting.
Chest landmarks by palpation; limb electrodes on wrists and ankles, not the chest.

elimination.verdict: A, B, E.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the lead II rhythm strip of an adult client with a regular heart rate of 78 beats per minute (expected adult range 60 to 100 beats per minute). Each QRS complex points upward from the baseline. In lead II, the positive electrode is the [[1]].

The upright QRS shows that the depolarization wave is traveling [[2]].

If a depolarization wave traveled at right angles to lead II, the nurse would expect [[3]] in that lead.

options.text: Left leg electrode
options.rationale: Lead II runs from the right arm, which is negative, to the left leg, which is positive.

options.text: Right arm electrode
options.rationale: The right arm electrode is part of lead II, but it is the negative electrode.

options.text: Left arm electrode
options.rationale: The left arm electrode is not one of the two electrodes that form lead II.

options.text: Right leg electrode
options.rationale: The right leg electrode is neutral. It is not the positive electrode for any lead.

options.text: From the upper right of the heart toward the lower left
options.rationale: Lead II runs from the right arm (negative) to the left leg (positive), so a wave moving down and to the left travels toward the positive electrode and deflects up.

options.text: From the lower left of the heart toward the upper right
options.rationale: This is movement toward the negative electrode, which deflects down.

options.text: From left to right across the top of the heart
options.rationale: This runs nearly at right angles to lead II and produces little or no deflection.

options.text: No deflection
options.rationale: A wave moving perpendicular to a lead produces no deflection in that lead.

options.text: A small positive deflection
options.rationale: A positive deflection needs movement toward the positive electrode. A wave at right angles moves neither toward nor away from it.

options.text: A negative deflection
options.rationale: A negative deflection needs movement away from the positive electrode. A wave at right angles moves neither toward nor away from it.

options.text: A deflection the same size as the QRS
options.rationale: Deflection size is proportional to the wave seen by that lead. A wave at right angles produces none.

questions.takeaway: Lead II: right arm negative, left leg positive, right leg neutral. A wave toward the positive electrode deflects up, away deflects down, at right angles gives no deflection, and the size is proportional.
questions.strategy: Fix the electrodes of lead II first. Once the positive electrode is known, the direction of each deflection follows from where the wave is moving relative to it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lead II: right arm negative, left leg positive.
Upright means toward the positive electrode, so the wave runs from upper right to lower left.
At right angles: neither toward nor away, so no deflection.

elimination.verdict: Left leg electrode; from the upper right of the heart toward the lower left; no deflection.

questions.scenario: A nurse auscultates the heart of an adult client lying back. The apical pulse is 72 beats per minute and regular (expected adult range 60 to 100 beats per minute). The nurse hears a long, loud first sound followed by a short, sharp second sound at each beat and relates each event below to the cardiac cycle.
questions.stem: For each event, indicate the phase of the cardiac cycle in which it occurs.

rows.text: The mitral and tricuspid valves are open
rows.rationale: The mitral and tricuspid valves close at the start of systole. They are open during diastole, while the relaxed ventricles fill.

rows.text: The atria contract to complete ventricular filling
rows.rationale: Atrial contraction happens at the end of diastole, before the first heart sound. It is a contraction, but it is not systole.

rows.text: The aortic and pulmonary valves are open
rows.rationale: During systole the ventricles contract and the aortic and pulmonary valves open to let blood leave the heart.

rows.text: The left ventricle pumps oxygen rich blood into the systemic circuit
rows.rationale: Blood leaves the left ventricle for the body when the ventricles contract, which is systole.

rows.text: The phase that begins as the short, sharp second sound is heard
rows.rationale: The second heart sound is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, which marks the start of diastole.

questions.takeaway: Systole: ventricles contract, aortic and pulmonary valves open, blood ejected. Diastole: ventricles relax and fill, with atrial contraction at the end. S2 marks the start of diastole.
questions.strategy: Classify each event by what the ventricles are doing, not by whether something is contracting. The atria contract while the ventricles are still in diastole.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contracting is systole; relaxed and filling is diastole.
Atrial contraction is the end of diastole.
The second sound is the aortic and pulmonary valves closing, so diastole begins.

elimination.verdict: Open mitral and tricuspid valves and atrial contraction are diastole. Open aortic and pulmonary valves and ejection to the body are systole. The second sound starts diastole.

questions.stem: An adult client was admitted 2 days ago with pneumonia. The right radial pulse has been documented at 64 to 70 beats per minute, regular, at every check since admission. At 1400 the nurse finds: right radial pulse 98 beats per minute, regular (expected adult range 60 to 100 beats per minute); oxygen saturation 95% on room air (expected 95% to 100%); capillary refill in the right hand 2 seconds (expected 2 seconds or less); blood pressure 116/72 mm Hg (expected adult range below 120/80 mm Hg). Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Document the findings as within the expected ranges and recheck them at the next scheduled set of observations
options.rationale: Each value sits inside its expected range, but the pulse has risen by 28 to 34 beats per minute from this client's own documented rate. Pulse assessment gives a baseline so that change can be identified, and waiting hides that change.

options.text: Reassess the client now, including the respiratory rate, and report the rise from the client's usual pulse rate
options.rationale: The pulse has risen from 64 to 70 beats per minute at every check to 98 beats per minute. A change from the client's own baseline is acted on even when the number is still in range, so the nurse reassesses and reports it.

options.text: Recount the right radial pulse, and document the result as within range if it is again below 100 beats per minute
options.rationale: Rechecking is reasonable, but the plan accepts any rate below 100 beats per minute. It still compares the pulse only with the adult range, not with this client's rate of 64 to 70 beats per minute.

options.text: Apply oxygen at 2 L per minute, because the saturation is at the lower limit of the expected range
options.rationale: The saturation of 95% is within the expected range, and starting oxygen treats one number before the client has been reassessed. The finding that has changed is the pulse.

questions.takeaway: Pulse is assessed alongside oxygen saturation, blood pressure and capillary refill, and it gives a baseline of what is usual for the client. A clear change from that baseline needs action even when every value is still within the expected range.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible because every value is in range. The deciding cue in the stem is the documented rate of 64 to 70 beats per minute at every check since admission.

steps.detail: Every value is within its expected range.
Pulse 98 against a usual 64 to 70 beats per minute: a clear change.
Documenting, or recounting against 100 beats per minute, ignores the baseline.
Oxygen for a saturation inside the range skips reassessment.

elimination.verdict: Reassess now and report the rise from the client's usual pulse rate.

questions.stem: A client is admitted after a fall with a head injury. Blood pressure is 96/58 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), heart rate is 112 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and serum sodium is 140 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145 mEq/L). The provider orders 0.45% sodium chloride at 125 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Start the infusion at 125 mL per hour and check neurologic status every hour
options.rationale: Hourly neurologic checks are good care, but 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic. It moves water into cells, including brain cells, and it is contraindicated with head trauma and low blood pressure.

options.text: Start the infusion at 75 mL per hour, a slower rate, until the provider rounds
options.rationale: A slower rate still moves water into brain cells. The problem is the type of fluid, not the speed.

options.text: Hold the infusion and contact the provider to question the order before starting it
options.rationale: Hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with head trauma, raised pressure in the skull and low blood pressure. This client has a head injury, a blood pressure of 96/58 mm Hg with the diastolic below 60 mm Hg, and a heart rate of 112 beats per minute, so the order is questioned before it starts.

options.text: Hang 0.9% sodium chloride at 125 mL per hour instead, since both are saline
options.rationale: An isotonic fluid may well be what this client needs, but the nurse cannot change the type of fluid without an order.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluid (0.45% or 0.225% sodium chloride) moves water into cells. Do not give it with head trauma, raised pressure in the skull, low blood pressure or third spacing. Question the order before starting.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options give the ordered fluid and one changes it without an order. Ask what the fluid does once it is in the vein, then match that against the head injury.

steps.detail: 0.45% sodium chloride is hypotonic.
Into cells, including brain cells.
Head injury and a diastolic pressure below 60 mm Hg: both are contraindications.
Question the order. Do not swap fluids without one.

elimination.verdict: Hold the hypotonic fluid and question the order.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the IV fluid orders for six clients on a medical surgical unit.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate whether the ordered fluid is appropriate or the order should be questioned.

rows.text: A client bleeding after a car crash, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), ordered 0.9% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Isotonic fluid stays in the vessels and is used for volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation.

rows.text: A client with new confusion and serum sodium 118 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145 mEq/L), ordered 3% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: 3% sodium chloride is the hypertonic fluid for severe hyponatremia. Sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are watched closely.

rows.text: A client with ascites from fluid shifting into the abdomen, ordered 0.45% sodium chloride
rows.rationale: Third spacing is a contraindication to hypotonic fluid. More water would leave the vessels.

rows.text: A client with blood glucose 48 mg/dL (reference 70 to 100 mg/dL), ordered D10W
rows.rationale: D10W is a hypertonic dextrose solution used for hypoglycemia.

rows.text: A client with intracranial pressure 24 mm Hg (reference 5 to 15 mm Hg), ordered D5W as the continuous maintenance fluid
rows.rationale: Once the body uses the dextrose, D5W leaves free water. It acts as a hypotonic fluid and moves water into brain cells.

rows.text: A client about to receive packed red blood cells, ordered Lactated Ringer's to prime the blood tubing
rows.rationale: Blood products run with 0.9% sodium chloride only.

questions.takeaway: Match the fluid to where the water goes. Isotonic stays in the vessels, hypertonic pulls water out of cells, hypotonic pushes water into cells. D5W behaves as hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Judge each row on its own. For each fluid ask where the water goes, then ask whether that helps or harms this client.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 0.9% isotonic. 3% and D10W hypertonic. 0.45% hypotonic. D5W acts as hypotonic once the dextrose is used.
Third spacing and raised intracranial pressure rule out hypotonic fluid.
0.9% sodium chloride only with blood.

elimination.verdict: Appropriate: rows 1, 2 and 4. Question: rows 3, 5 and 6.

questions.stem: A client with diabetic ketoacidosis arrived in the emergency department with blood pressure 82/50 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg) and received 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride. On arrival to the unit, blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg, heart rate is 92 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), the client is alert and oriented, and serum sodium is 147 mEq/L (reference 135 to 145 mEq/L). The provider orders 0.45% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Question the order, because hypotonic fluid is contraindicated with low blood pressure
options.rationale: Low blood pressure is a contraindication while it is present. The blood pressure was 82/50 mm Hg in the emergency department and is now 118/72 mm Hg after 2 L of isotonic fluid.

options.text: Start the infusion and monitor serum sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance
options.rationale: In diabetic ketoacidosis, hypotonic fluid follows the initial isotonic resuscitation. The blood pressure is in range, the client is alert and the sodium is high, so the order fits. Sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance are the checks.

options.text: Ask the provider to change the order to Lactated Ringer's to protect the blood pressure
options.rationale: Isotonic fluid was the first step and the blood pressure has recovered. Lactated Ringer's does not give the cells the free water a sodium of 147 mEq/L calls for.

options.text: Hold the infusion until a repeat serum sodium result comes back from the lab
options.rationale: The sodium is already known to be above range. Waiting delays the ordered next step of the fluid plan.

questions.takeaway: Diabetic ketoacidosis fluid plan: isotonic fluid first to restore volume, then hypotonic fluid once the blood pressure has recovered. Hypotonic fluid is unsafe while blood pressure is low.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options seem defensible: start the hypotonic fluid, or question it because of the emergency department blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg. The deciding cue is the current blood pressure, 118/72 mm Hg.

steps.action: Find where the client is in the plan
steps.detail: 2 L of isotonic fluid already given.
Blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg: no longer low.
147 mEq/L: water is needed in the cells.
Lactated Ringer's adds no free water. Waiting for a repeat sodium delays care.

elimination.verdict: Start the hypotonic fluid and monitor sodium, neurologic status and fluid balance.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red blood cells arrives on the unit for a client with hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL (reference 12 to 17.5 g/dL). Consent is on file, baseline vital signs are recorded, and two nurses have verified the unit at the bedside. The client has a 22 gauge IV in the left hand with Lactated Ringer's infusing. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Start an 18 or 20 gauge IV and prime the blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Blood needs an 18 or 20 gauge catheter and 0.9% sodium chloride only. This solves both problems with the current line.

options.text: Prime the blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride and run the unit through the 22 gauge IV
options.rationale: The solution is now right, but a 22 gauge catheter is smaller than the 18 to 20 gauge needed for blood.

options.text: Run the unit through the existing line, since two nurses have already verified it
options.rationale: Verification is complete, but the line is the wrong size and Lactated Ringer's cannot run with blood.

options.text: Keep the unit at the bedside until a new IV can be placed at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Packed red cells must be infused within 4 hours of issue. A new line is needed now, not later in the shift.

questions.takeaway: Every blood product needs two nurse verification, an 18 to 20 gauge catheter and 0.9% sodium chloride only. Packed red cells are infused within 4 hours of issue.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: The verification is done, which makes using the current line tempting. Check two things in each option: the catheter size and the solution.

steps.detail: 22 gauge is too small. Blood needs 18 to 20.
Lactated Ringer's cannot run with blood.
4 hours from issue: do not wait until the end of the shift.

elimination.verdict: New 18 or 20 gauge line, primed with 0.9% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to give a unit of packed red blood cells. Baseline vital signs have been recorded. Place the steps in order.

options.text: Reassess vital signs 15 minutes after the transfusion starts
options.rationale: The first reassessment is at 15 minutes, when a reaction is most likely to show.

options.text: Confirm that signed consent is on file
options.rationale: Consent must be on file before the unit is picked up from the blood bank.

options.text: Check the unit against the identification band with a second nurse at the bedside
options.rationale: Two licensed nurses verify the label, blood type, unit number and expiration date before the start.

options.text: Pick up the unit from the blood bank
options.rationale: The unit is collected only after consent is confirmed.

options.text: Start the transfusion
options.rationale: The unit starts after the bedside check.

options.text: Reassess vital signs every 30 to 60 minutes until the unit is complete
options.rationale: After the 15 minute check, vital signs continue every 30 to 60 minutes and at completion.

questions.takeaway: Blood order: consent on file, then pick up the unit, then two nurse bedside check, then start, then vital signs at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes and at completion.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Anchor the first and last steps. Consent comes before the unit leaves the blood bank, and the 15 minute check can only come after the start.

steps.detail: Consent before the unit is retrieved.
The second nurse check is at the bedside, before the start.
Vital signs 15 minutes after the start, then every 30 to 60 minutes.

elimination.verdict: Consent, pick up, two nurse check, start, recheck at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes.
