questions.nursesNote: 0900, right forearm 20 gauge IV with 0.9% sodium chloride ordered at 100 mL per hour: Skin around the site is cool and pale. Edema extends 4 cm from the site. The drip rate has slowed. No blood return on aspiration. No redness or streak along the vein. Temperature is 36.8 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Capillary refill in the right fingers is 2 seconds (reference less than 3 seconds).
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate infiltration.

segments.text: Skin around the site is cool and pale
segments.rationale: Fluid in the tissue cools the skin and makes it pale: a sign of infiltration.

segments.text: Edema extends 4 cm from the site
segments.rationale: Fluid leaking into the tissue causes swelling around the site.

segments.text: The drip rate has slowed
segments.rationale: Fluid going into the tissue meets resistance, so the drip slows.

segments.text: No blood return on aspiration
segments.rationale: The catheter tip is no longer in the vein.

segments.text: No redness or streak along the vein
segments.rationale: Redness and a streak are signs of phlebitis. Their absence does not point to infiltration.

segments.text: Temperature is 36.8 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C)
segments.rationale: A normal temperature is not a sign of infiltration.

segments.text: Capillary refill in the right fingers is 2 seconds (reference less than 3 seconds)
segments.rationale: Normal capillary refill shows circulation beyond the site is intact. It is not a sign of infiltration.

questions.takeaway: Infiltration: cool, pale skin, edema, a slowed drip and no blood return. Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a streak and a cord along the vein.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Sort each finding into infiltration, phlebitis or normal. Only the infiltration findings are highlighted.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cool, pale, swollen.
Slowed drip, no blood return.
No phlebitis signs, normal temperature, normal capillary refill.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: A client is receiving an IV antibiotic through a 20 gauge catheter in the left forearm. The nurse finds mild swelling at the site, redness and warmth along the vein, a red streak 3 cm above the site, and a firm cord when the vein is palpated. Pain at the site is 5 of 10. The infusion is running at the ordered rate and there is a blood return. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Flush the catheter with 0.9% sodium chloride, since the blood return shows it is still in the vein
options.rationale: The blood return rules out infiltration, but redness, warmth, a streak and a cord mean the vein wall is inflamed. The catheter does not stay.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, elevate the left arm and apply a compress chosen for the antibiotic
options.rationale: This is the infiltration plan. Swelling is present, but the skin is warm and red with a streak and a cord, not cool and pale, and blood still returns. That points to phlebitis.

options.text: Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress and notify the provider
options.rationale: Redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord are phlebitis. The plan is stop, remove, warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.

options.text: Stop the infusion, keep the catheter for the next dose and apply a warm moist compress
options.rationale: The compress is right, but a catheter in an inflamed vein is removed, not saved.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis: pain, redness, warmth, a streak and a palpable cord. Stop, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider and document the grade.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options stop and remove the catheter. The swelling suggests infiltration. The deciding cue is warm, red skin with a cord and a blood return, which means phlebitis, not the cool, pale skin of infiltration.

steps.detail: Red, warm, streak, cord: phlebitis.
A blood return does not make an inflamed vein safe.
Warm moist compress and notify for phlebitis. Elevate and compress by solution for infiltration.

elimination.verdict: Stop, remove, warm moist compress, notify the provider.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.scenario: The tubing of a client's central line separates at the hub while the client is sitting up in a chair. Within a minute the client reports sudden shortness of breath and chest pain. Blood pressure is 82/48 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), heart rate is 124 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and oxygen saturation is 86% (reference 95% to 100%). A churning sound is heard over the heart.
questions.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 condition the client is most likely experiencing, and 2 parameters the nurse monitors.

options.text: Clamp the catheter
options.rationale: Clamping stops more air from entering the vein.

options.text: Return the client to bed on the left side with the head down
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps the air in the right side of the heart, away from the lungs.

options.text: Lay the client flat on the back with the legs raised
options.rationale: A shock position does not trap the air in the right side of the heart. The left side with the head down does.

options.text: Flush the line with 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Flushing pushes more of what is in the line into the vein.

options.text: Remove the central line
options.rationale: The line is clamped, not removed, in this emergency.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: An open line, sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure and a churning sound over the heart.

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a fast infusion, with flushing, headache and chest tightness. Nothing was infusing fast.

options.text: Catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Infection brings fever and chills over time, not a sudden onset after a disconnection.

options.text: Fluid overload
options.rationale: Fluid overload builds over hours of infusion. This began within a minute of the line opening.

options.text: Oxygen saturation
options.rationale: 86% shows the air is blocking blood flow to the lungs.

options.text: Blood pressure
options.rationale: 82/48 mm Hg shows the heart is struggling to pump.

options.text: Temperature
options.rationale: Temperature does not track an air embolism.

options.text: Appearance of the insertion site
options.rationale: The problem is in the heart and lungs, not at the skin.

options.text: Urine specific gravity
options.rationale: This does not guide care in the next minutes.

questions.takeaway: Air embolism: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, low blood pressure and a churning murmur after air enters a line. Clamp the tubing, turn onto the left side head down, call rapid response and give 100% oxygen.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Link the timing to the event: an open central line, then sudden breathing and chest symptoms. Then choose actions that stop more air and keep the air away from the lungs.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Central line open at the hub.
Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, a churning sound.
Clamp.
Left side, head down.
Oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

elimination.verdict: Clamp the catheter and turn onto the left side head down. Air embolism. Watch oxygen saturation and blood pressure.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client who is going home with a PICC in the left arm. The client's temperature at discharge is 36.8 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C). Which statements by the client show correct understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will put a waterproof cover over the site when I shower."
options.rationale: Showering is allowed with a waterproof cover over the site.

options.text: "Once the site heals, I can swim laps at the pool again."
options.rationale: The arm is not submerged: no swimming and no baths while the PICC is in.

options.text: "No one should take my blood pressure on my left arm."
options.rationale: No blood pressure cuffs and no needle sticks on the PICC arm.

options.text: "If the flush is hard to push, I will push a little harder to clear it."
options.rationale: Resistance during a flush means stop and do not use the line. Force can break the catheter.

options.text: "I will call if my temperature reaches 38.2 °C."
options.rationale: A fever above 38 °C is a warning sign to report at once.

options.text: "I can carry my 20 lb laundry basket with my left arm."
options.rationale: Heavy lifting over 10 lb with the PICC arm is avoided.

questions.takeaway: PICC teaching: keep the dressing dry, shower with a cover, no swimming, no blood pressure cuff or needle sticks on that arm, nothing over 10 lb, never force a flush, and report a fever above 38 °C.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Treat each statement as true or false against the PICC rules: water, that arm, lifting, flushing and fever.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shower with a cover. No swimming.
No blood pressure cuff, no lifting over 10 lb.
Resistance means stop.
Above 38 °C: call.

elimination.verdict: A, C, E.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.stem: A registered nurse is assigning work to a licensed practical nurse (LPN) and assistive personnel (AP) on a medical surgical unit. Which task is appropriate for the registered nurse to delegate?

options.text: Ask the LPN to hang a unit of platelets after the registered nurse has checked it
options.rationale: Starting any blood product stays with the registered nurse, even after the check.

options.text: Ask the AP to look at a client's IV site and decide whether the catheter should come out
options.rationale: The AP can report how a site looks. Deciding what the finding means is the registered nurse's judgment.

options.text: Ask the LPN to start a new heparin infusion for a client admitted an hour ago
options.rationale: Heparin is a high alert IV medication, which the registered nurse gives.

options.text: Ask the LPN to flush the established IV line of a client ready for discharge
options.rationale: Flushing an established line is within the LPN's role, per the state practice act. The registered nurse stays accountable.

questions.takeaway: The registered nurse keeps insertion, site selection, starting blood, high alert IV drugs, interpreting findings and teaching. The LPN can monitor sites, flush established lines and hang non high alert fluids. AP take vital signs and report what a site looks like.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Each option hands off a real task. Ask whether the task needs judgment, starts blood or involves a high alert drug.

steps.detail: Platelets: registered nurse.
Deciding a catheter comes out: registered nurse.
Heparin: registered nurse.
Flushing an established line: LPN.

elimination.verdict: Delegate the flush of an established line to the LPN.

questions.objective: RN Responsibility & Delegation

questions.scenario: A nurse on a medical surgical unit reviews the access plans for six adult clients. No ordered drug is a vesicant unless the row says so.
questions.stem: For each client, indicate the least invasive access device that fits the therapy.

rows.text: A client needs 0.9% sodium chloride for 2 days after a minor surgery
rows.rationale: Short term isotonic fluid can run through a short peripheral IV. Nothing about this therapy calls for a longer device.

rows.text: A client will go home on a non vesicant IV antibiotic for 3 weeks
rows.rationale: Therapy longer than 6 days warrants a midline or PICC. A midline can dwell up to 4 weeks and suits non vesicant antibiotics, so it is the less invasive choice. A PICC would work but is more than this therapy needs.

rows.text: A client needs total parenteral nutrition for 6 weeks
rows.rationale: Total parenteral nutrition requires central access. A midline is not used for it, however long it can dwell.

rows.text: A client will receive a vesicant chemotherapy drug every 3 weeks for 6 months
rows.rationale: Vesicants require central access. Long term intermittent therapy like this is where an implanted port fits.

rows.text: A client in the intensive care unit needs a continuous vasopressor infusion that is expected to last several days
rows.rationale: A midline is not used for continuous vasopressors. Over several days a continuous vasopressor needs central access.

rows.text: A client needs an IV analgesic for 2 weeks, and the forearm veins are scarred from repeated sticks
rows.rationale: Two weeks is longer than 6 days, analgesics are a listed midline use, and one midline spares the scarred veins from repeated short peripheral sticks. A midline is inserted in an upper arm vein, above the scarred forearm veins.

questions.takeaway: Choose access by duration and solution. Short term isotonic fluid: short peripheral IV. Non vesicant therapy longer than 6 days, up to 4 weeks: midline. Vesicants, total parenteral nutrition, continuous vasopressors or long term therapy: central line.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Ask two questions for each row: how long, and what is going in. A vesicant or total parenteral nutrition sends the row straight to a central line, and a midline is never used for a continuous vasopressor.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Vesicant chemotherapy, total parenteral nutrition and a vasopressor running for several days need a central line.
2 days of isotonic fluid fits a short peripheral IV.

steps.action: Pick the least invasive device for the rest
steps.detail: 3 weeks of an antibiotic and 2 weeks of an analgesic are non vesicant and under 4 weeks: midline.

elimination.verdict: Short peripheral IV: row 1. Midline: rows 2 and 6. Central line: rows 3, 4 and 5.

questions.objective: Vascular Access Devices

questions.nursesNote: 1030. Client is 84 years old with lymphedema of the left arm after a left mastectomy. Ordered: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL per hour for 2 days. Peripheral IV insertion by a student nurse, observed by the registered nurse: Selected a 22 gauge catheter. Chose a soft, straight cephalic vein in the right forearm. Scrubbed the site with chlorhexidine using a back and forth motion for 30 seconds. Fanned the site with a hand to speed drying. Palpated the vein again after the prep to confirm the location. During advancement the client reported a sudden shooting pain into the right thumb, and the student finished advancing and secured the catheter. Listed a left dorsal hand vein as the backup site. Documented site, gauge, number of attempts and skin condition.
questions.stem: Highlight the actions that require follow up by the registered nurse.

segments.text: Selected a 22 gauge catheter
segments.rationale: A 22 to 24 gauge catheter is recommended for older adults with fragile veins and is enough for maintenance fluid.

segments.text: Chose a soft, straight cephalic vein in the right forearm
segments.rationale: A soft, straight forearm vein on the arm without lymphedema is the preferred choice.

segments.text: Scrubbed the site with chlorhexidine using a back and forth motion for 30 seconds
segments.rationale: Chlorhexidine applied with a back and forth scrub for at least 30 seconds is the correct prep.

segments.text: Fanned the site with a hand to speed drying
segments.rationale: The antiseptic must air dry completely. Fanning, blotting or wiping is not done.

segments.text: Palpated the vein again after the prep to confirm the location
segments.rationale: Touching the cleansed site again with unsterile fingers contaminates it and cancels the prep.

segments.text: During advancement the client reported a sudden shooting pain into the right thumb, and the student finished advancing and secured the catheter
segments.rationale: Shooting pain, burning, numbness or tingling during insertion signals nerve injury. Insertion stops immediately, the catheter is removed and neurologic function is assessed.

segments.text: Listed a left dorsal hand vein as the backup site
segments.rationale: The left arm is the lymphedema arm after mastectomy, which is avoided. Dorsal hand veins are also avoided in older adults when possible.

segments.text: Documented site, gauge, number of attempts and skin condition
segments.rationale: These are required elements of insertion documentation, and skin condition is documented before and after every access attempt in older adults.

questions.takeaway: Air dry the chlorhexidine without fanning, never touch the site again after prep, stop at once for shooting pain or tingling during insertion, and avoid the arm on the mastectomy side and the dorsal hand in older adults.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Read each action against three checklists: the skin prep steps, the sites to avoid and the nerve injury signs. Highlight only what breaks a rule.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Scrub for 30 seconds is right. Fanning and touching the site again are wrong.
Right forearm is right. Left arm and dorsal hand are wrong for this client.
Shooting pain during advancement means stop, not finish.
22 gauge and complete documentation need no follow up.

questions.objective: Safety Protocols

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A client in the intensive care unit has had a nontunneled central line in the right internal jugular vein for 6 days. Oral temperature is 38.6 °C (reference 36.1 to 37.2 °C), heart rate is 118 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg). The client has shaking chills and is newly disoriented to time. Lungs are clear, the urine is clear, and the insertion site has no redness or drainage. The infusion is running by pump at the ordered rate.

The client's findings are most consistent with [[1]].

The nurse anticipates [[2]] as the initial treatment.

If a new nontunneled central line is needed, the site the prevention bundle prefers when possible is the [[3]] vein.

options.text: Catheter related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: Fever, chills, low blood pressure and altered mental status with no other source in a client with a central line point to a catheter related bloodstream infection. The clear lungs, clear urine and clean site rule out other sources.

options.text: Phlebitis at the insertion site
options.rationale: Phlebitis shows at the vein: redness, warmth, a streak or a cord. The site has no redness.

options.text: Speed shock from the infusion
options.rationale: Speed shock follows a rapid infusion, with flushing, headache and chest tightness. The pump is running at the ordered rate.

options.text: Air embolism through the catheter
options.rationale: Air embolism brings sudden shortness of breath and chest pain. It does not bring fever and chills.

options.text: Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Treatment is blood cultures twice, IV antibiotics, and catheter removal if needed.

options.text: One set of blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Antibiotics are right, but blood cultures are drawn twice, not once.

options.text: A warm moist compress over the insertion site
options.rationale: This is a phlebitis intervention. The infection here is in the bloodstream, not at the vein wall.

options.text: A slower infusion rate set on the pump
options.rationale: Slowing the rate prevents speed shock. It does nothing for an infection.

options.text: Subclavian
options.rationale: The bundle prefers the subclavian site over the internal jugular or femoral site when possible.

options.text: Internal jugular
options.rationale: The bundle ranks the internal jugular below the subclavian site.

options.text: Femoral
options.rationale: The femoral site carries the highest infection risk of the three.

questions.takeaway: Catheter related bloodstream infection: fever, chills, hypotension and altered mental status with no other source. Draw blood cultures twice, start IV antibiotics and remove the catheter if needed. Prevent it with hand hygiene, maximal barriers, chlorhexidine prep, the subclavian site when possible and a daily review of whether the line is still needed.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: First rule out every other source the stem hands you: lungs, urine, site and rate. What is left with a central line is the bloodstream infection. Then match each treatment option to the complication it belongs to.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Clear lungs, clear urine, clean site: the line is the source.
No redness for phlebitis, ordered rate for speed shock, no sudden breathing change for air embolism.
Twice, not once.
Subclavian preferred, femoral highest risk.

elimination.verdict: Catheter related bloodstream infection. Two sets of blood cultures and IV antibiotics. Subclavian.

questions.objective: Recognize Complications

questions.stem: An 87 year old client receiving hospice care in a long term care facility has had poor oral intake for 3 days. The client is alert and oriented, blood pressure is 108/66 mm Hg (reference 90/60 to 120/80 mm Hg), heart rate is 96 beats per minute (reference 60 to 100 beats per minute), and the oral mucous membranes are dry. The provider orders fluid replacement. Three peripheral IV attempts with a vein illumination device have failed. Ultrasound guided insertion is not available at the facility and would require transfer to the hospital. The hospice plan of care documents the client's wish to avoid hospital transfer. Which route does the nurse recommend to the provider?

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen at a rate of about 1 mL per minute
options.rationale: Subcutaneous infusion is used for mild to moderate dehydration in older and palliative clients and is avoided only in severe dehydration or shock. The abdomen is a common site and about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate. It needs no transfer.

options.text: Transfer to the hospital for ultrasound guided IV insertion, the standard for difficult access
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the standard for difficult access, but it requires a transfer the client has declined, and mild to moderate dehydration in a palliative client can be treated subcutaneously.

options.text: Subcutaneous infusion into the thigh at a rate of about 5 mL per minute
options.rationale: The route and site are right, but about 1 mL per minute is the maximum rate for subcutaneous infusion.

options.text: Intraosseous access in the proximal tibia, since it delivers all IV fluids
options.rationale: Intraosseous access does deliver all IV fluids when IV access fails, but it is for emergencies such as cardiac arrest or trauma and is limited to 24 hours. This client is alert with a blood pressure in range.

questions.takeaway: When IV access fails, match the alternative to the client's goals and urgency. Ultrasound guided insertion is the standard for difficult access. Subcutaneous infusion (hypodermoclysis) suits mild to moderate dehydration in older or palliative clients at about 1 mL per minute and is avoided in severe dehydration or shock. Intraosseous access is for emergencies and is limited to 24 hours.
questions.coverage: Covered in the Infusion Therapy lecture slides.
questions.strategy: Two options are defensible: ultrasound guided IV insertion, the standard for difficult access, and subcutaneous infusion. The deciding cue is the documented wish to avoid hospital transfer, with findings that show neither severe dehydration nor shock.

steps.detail: Alert, blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg, heart rate 96 beats per minute: not shock, not an emergency.
Ultrasound requires a hospital transfer the client has declined.
Intraosseous access is for cardiac arrest, trauma or pediatric emergencies and lasts 24 hours at most.
Same route, but the rate limit is about 1 mL per minute, not 5.

elimination.verdict: Subcutaneous infusion into the abdomen at about 1 mL per minute.
